name: Cheetah
blurb: A long-legged spotted cat built like a sprinter, and the fastest runner on land.
size: Nose to tail, about as long as a doorway is tall — but lean. A big one weighs roughly what a German shepherd weighs.

facts.text: The fastest cheetah ever timed ran 100 meters in 5.95 seconds. The human world record is 9.58. She beat the fastest man alive by more than three seconds.
facts.more: Her name was Sarah and she lived at the Cincinnati Zoo. She was chasing a fluffy lure on a rope, and she hit a peak of 61 mph (98 km/h) on the run.

facts.text: At full sprint one cheetah stride covers up to 23 feet (7 m) — two small cars parked end to end — and it takes four of them every second.
facts.more: Cheetah top speed gets exaggerated constantly. The highest reliably measured is 65 mph (104 km/h). A famous figure of 71 mph came from a faulty measuring method and was thrown out.

facts.text: Stand a cheetah next to a leopard and the cheetah looks bigger. Weigh them and it isn't. Small head, deep chest, legs like stilts: long and light, not heavy.
A cheetah's claws never fully pull in. They have no protective sheath, so they stay out and blunt, biting into the ground like a sprinter's spikes.
facts.more: Nearly every other cat keeps its claws sheathed and razor-sharp for fighting. The cheetah's are permanently out and permanently dull. Grip matters more than sharpness when you are moving that fast.

facts.text: The tail is a rudder. Watch a cheetah corner at speed and the tail swings the opposite way, flinging the body round the turn without a tumble.
facts.more: GPS collars on wild cheetahs in Botswana recorded hundreds of hunts and found they are won by grip and turning, not top speed. The average hunting run reached only 34 mph (54 km/h).

facts.text: Pound for pound, a wild cheetah accelerating puts out about four times the power Usain Bolt produces at full sprint — and double that of a polo pony at a gallop.
facts.more: Those same Botswana collars carried motion sensors as well as GPS. The figures they logged for acceleration, braking and turning force are the highest ever measured on a wild land mammal.

facts.text: A cheetah's retina carries a long horizontal band of sharp-vision cells, so the whole width of the grassland stays crisp at once, like a permanent panoramic camera.
A cheetah cannot roar. It chirps like a bird. A mother calling her cubs makes a high yelping sound you would swear came from something with feathers.
facts.more: Cats fall into two camps: the ones that roar — lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar — and the ones that purr. The cheetah is firmly in the purring camp, and its purr is far louder than a house cat's.

facts.text: It hunts in daylight, while lions and hyenas are sleeping off the heat. Speed is no use to you if something bigger simply walks over and takes your dinner.
facts.more: Stealing another animal's kill has a name: kleptoparasitism. Cheetahs lose kills to it constantly, so they eat fast and rarely stay with a carcass. After a flat-out run a cheetah has to lie panting for many minutes before it can even begin.

facts.text: Huge nostrils, huge lungs, huge heart. A sprinting cheetah is essentially an air pump with legs.
facts.more: The nasal openings are so wide there is little room left in the skull for long tooth roots, so a cheetah's canines are small and conical. It kills by clamping the windpipe shut and holding on, not by stabbing.

facts.text: Cheetah cubs grow a cape of long smoky-gray hair down the back and shoulders, shaggy enough to hide the spots underneath. Researchers call it a mantle.
facts.more: It thins out and disappears as the cub grows. Until then a cub looks almost nothing like the sleek animal it will become — more like a scruffy gray tuft with a cat's face.

facts.text: No two cheetahs are spotted the same way. Field researchers photograph faces and flanks and identify individuals by pattern, the way police use fingerprints.

wonder: Claws that never sheathe, a tail that steers, eyes that hold the horizon still — every separate part of this animal pointing the same direction.

name: Snow leopard
blurb: A pale smoke-gray cat with an enormous tail that lives higher up the mountains than almost any other large animal.
size: About the size of a Labrador, plus a tail nearly as long again as the rest of it.

facts.text: The tail is the giveaway. Up to 3 feet (1 m) long — nearly as long as the rest of the cat, and thick as a fire hose with fur and stored fat.
facts.more: It works as a balance bar on ledges barely wider than a paw. At rest the snow leopard curls it over its own face like a scarf.

facts.text: For a big cat it is small: about 100 lb (45 kg), the weight of a Labrador. The paws and the tail look several sizes too big for the body they came with.
A snow leopard cannot roar — its vocal folds are too short. Its greeting is a chuff: a puff of air pushed out through the nose, half snort, half soft sneeze.
Its paws are enormous and furred underneath, spreading its weight across snow like a pair of built-in snowshoes.
It breathes thin, freezing air at 10,000 feet (3,000 m) and higher. Its nasal cavity is unusually large, so air is warmed on the way in before it ever reaches the lungs.
facts.more: Its whole range sits between about 9,800 and 14,800 feet (3,000 to 4,500 m) — higher than almost any other large predator goes, on air with a third less oxygen in it than the air at the beach.

facts.text: A snow leopard regularly kills prey heavier than itself: wild sheep and ibex of 80 to 165 lb (36 to 76 kg), brought down where one slip means a very long fall.
facts.more: Its favorite prey, the blue sheep, lives on cliffs. The cat stalks from above, drops, and grabs. Then it stays with the kill for days, eating slowly, because the next meal might be a week away.

facts.text: The pounce is only the start. Carrying the momentum of that first leap, a snow leopard has been tracked chasing prey 980 feet (300 m) down a mountainside.
facts.more: That is the length of three football pitches, made of loose rock, snow and drop-offs, taken at a run by an animal that has already thrown itself off a ledge and cannot change its mind.

facts.text: Pale gray fur smudged with dark rosettes. Photographs of snow leopards on bare rock get passed around as puzzles, because people genuinely cannot find the cat.
facts.more: The pattern breaks the outline up. Instead of one cat-shaped thing you see scattered patches of light and shadow, which is exactly what a scree slope already looks like.

facts.text: It is called the ghost of the mountains, and not as a compliment to its manners. Researchers can work in snow leopard country for months and see nothing but tracks.
facts.more: Almost everything we know comes from camera traps and GPS collars rather than from watching. Even the rosette patterns used to tell one cat from another are read off automatic photographs.

facts.text: Cubs are born blind in a rock den that the mother lines with fur pulled from her own belly. They do not step outside it for two to four months.
Its fur grows up to 5 inches (12 cm) long, deepest of all on the belly, so the cat can lie down flat on snow and stay warm.
One cat may patrol a home range larger than a city, and in mountains that steep the distance is measured in climbing rather than walking.

wonder: Nobody is watching when that tail wraps over that face on a frozen ledge at 12,000 feet. It was made beautiful anyway.

name: Tiger
blurb: The largest cat in the world: a striped ambush hunter that works alone and swims for pleasure.
size: A big male weighs about as much as three grown men, and stretches longer nose to tail than a door is tall.

facts.text: No cat alive is bigger. A large male tiger weighs about as much as three grown men, and leaves a front paw print the size of a side plate.
Shave a tiger and the stripes are still there. The pattern is in the skin itself, not only in the fur.
facts.more: And every tiger's pattern is unique — not shared by littermates, not shared by mother and cub, not even matching between the left and right sides of the same tiger. Researchers photograph both flanks and identify individuals from the stripes alone.

facts.text: Its upper canine teeth are the longest of any cat alive: up to 3 inches (7.6 cm), roughly the length of a grown-up's middle finger.
A tiger can stalk for an hour, creep to within 30 feet (9 m), and still end the night hungry. Far more hunts fail than succeed — by some counts nine in ten.
facts.more: Which is why a kill matters so much. A tiger can eat 110 pounds (50 kg) of meat in one sitting — close to a quarter of its own body weight — then drag what is left into thick cover and come back to it for days.

facts.text: Orange and black looks loud to you. To a deer it does not — deer cannot see orange, so a tiger in dry grass reads as nothing but broken lines of shadow.
facts.more: Deer see blues and yellows but not reds and oranges. The tiger's coat lands on them as roughly the same dull tone as the grass around it, cut into stripes that hide the shape of an animal.

facts.text: A tiger's roar carries about 2 miles (3 km) through forest. You would hear it long, long before you had any chance of seeing the animal that made it.
Most cats loathe water. Tigers swim well and often, lying in rivers for hours on hot days and crossing open channels as wide as 5 miles (8 km).
facts.more: In the mangrove forests of the Sundarbans, where the land is cut into pieces by tidal creeks, swimming is simply how a tiger gets to work.

facts.text: A tiger sees in near-darkness about six times better than you can. A mirror-like layer behind the retina bounces light back through the eye for a second pass — the same layer that makes cat eyes flash in a flashlight beam.
A tiger sprints about 35 mph (56 km/h), and not for long. All that weight is made for the ambush, not the chase: it has to be within a few bounds before it moves at all.
A tiger's tongue is covered in backward-pointing hooks stiff enough to rasp meat off bone. A few licks would take the skin off your arm.
Cubs are born blind and helpless, weighing about as much as a bag of flour, and stay with their mother for around two years learning how to hunt.
facts.more: Everything a tiger knows about stalking, choosing prey and killing cleanly is learned in those two years. A cub that leaves early usually cannot feed itself.

facts.text: A tiger patrols alone and marks the edges of its territory with scent and with claw rakes gouged deep into tree trunks — a message left for cats it may never meet.

wonder: The stripes run all the way down to the skin. Whoever made this animal did not stop at the part you can see.

name: Lion
blurb: The only cat that lives in a family group — and by a wide margin the loudest.
size: A big male's shoulder comes up to an adult's waist, and he weighs about as much as two and a half grown men.

facts.text: A lion's roar carries about 5 miles (8 km) across open country. Standing close to one is like standing beside a chainsaw that has opinions about you.
facts.more: The low pitch is the trick. Deep sound bends around trees and rocks instead of bouncing off them, so it keeps traveling long after a higher, shriller noise would have faded to nothing.

facts.text: Stand beside a big male and his shoulder reaches your waist. He weighs about as much as two and a half grown men, and most of that is neck, chest and jaw.
Researchers stood life-sized model lions out on the Serengeti to find out what a mane means. Females walked up to the dark-maned dummy. Males avoided it and picked on the blond one.
facts.more: Mane color turns out to track a male's condition — darker-maned lions carried more testosterone and were in better shape. The color is honest advertising, readable from a long way off, before anybody has to fight about it.

facts.text: Lions are the only cats that live in prides — permanent family groups of mostly related females. Grandmothers, mothers, sisters and daughters stay together for life.
The lionesses do most of the hunting, and they do it as a team: some circling wide to spook the prey, others waiting flat in the grass exactly where it will run.
facts.more: Hunting together lets a pride take on animals no single lion could handle, including buffalo. The males' job is mostly holding the territory against other males, which is dangerous work of a different kind.

facts.text: A lion may rest 20 hours out of every 24. In the afternoon heat a whole pride lies flat on its back in the shade like a pile of dropped laundry.
For all that power a lion is a sprinter, not a runner: about 35 mph (56 km/h) for a couple of hundred feet, and then it is finished. The hunt ends quickly or not at all.
Lion cubs are born covered in faint spots and rosettes that fade as they grow. For the first months a lion cub looks a little like a small leopard.
Cubs of similar ages are raised together in a crèche, and a lioness will let cubs that are not her own nurse from her.
facts.more: This is genuinely unusual. Most mammal mothers feed their own young and nobody else's. In a lion pride the females are close relatives, and the cubs are raised more or less as one batch.

facts.text: Every lion has its own pattern of whisker spots — the small dark dots the whiskers grow out of. Researchers use them to tell one lion from another in the field.
A lion is the only cat with a tuft on the end of its tail. Cubs are born without one; it grows in over their first year.
facts.more: Hidden inside the tuft on some lions is a hard little spur of skin about 5 mm long, roughly the size of a grain of rice. Nobody has worked out what it is for.

facts.text: Almost all wild lions live in Africa. One small population hangs on in the Gir Forest of India — the last wild lions anywhere else on earth.
facts.more: The Gir lions are slightly smaller, with sparser manes and a fold of skin along the belly. They live in dry teak forest rather than open savanna, sharing the ground with farms and villages.

wonder: Given a voice that carries five miles, and given a family worth using it on.

name: Fennec fox
blurb: The smallest fox in the world: a pale, enormous-eared desert dog that comes out at night.
size: Smaller than a house cat and light enough to lift in one hand — about the weight of a bag of sugar.

facts.text: The smallest fox on earth, and the smallest wild dog of any kind. A full-grown fennec weighs about 3 lb (1.3 kg) — you could hold one in two hands like a loaf of bread.
Its ears are the largest for body size of any dog, fox or wolf anywhere: nearly 4 inches (10 cm) tall, on an animal no bigger than a kitten.
A fennec hunts by listening. It stops dead, swivels its head one way and then the other, then digs straight down into open sand and comes up with something that was never visible at all.
facts.more: The prey is underground — beetles, grubs, lizards. The fennec is not guessing. Those ears pick up small movements beneath the surface, and the fox digs to the exact spot it heard.

facts.text: Those same ears are a cooling system. They are thin, with blood vessels running close to the surface, so heat leaves the blood and drifts away into the air.
A fennec can live where there is nothing to drink. It takes its water from the bodies of the animals it eats, and goes without whenever it has to.
facts.more: Its kidneys are large and dense, holding water back instead of spending it, so very little is lost. Offer a fennec a puddle and it will happily drink — it simply does not need one to survive.

facts.text: The soles of its feet are furred over. That is heat-proofing against sand hot enough to burn, and it doubles as grip — snowshoes, for sand.
It digs. In firm ground a fennec's den can sprawl across 120 square meters — about the floor of a small house — with as many as 15 separate doorways.
facts.more: In loose sand the den is far simpler, often with a single entrance, because the walls will not hold. Underground the air stays cool and slightly damp all day while the surface above it bakes.

facts.text: It sleeps through the heat and comes out at dusk. Nearly everything a fennec does — hunting, digging, squabbling, playing — happens in the dark.
Most foxes live alone. Fennecs live in family groups, share a den, and have been seen wrestling and chasing each other like puppies.
It is astonishingly noisy for its size — barking, yapping, squeaking and purring, with a voice you would expect from an animal ten times bigger.
It eats nearly anything small: insects, lizards, small birds and their eggs, rodents, and fruit, leaves and roots, which count as dinner and drink at the same time.
Its cream-colored coat matches the sand almost exactly. The same pale fur throws off sunlight during the day and holds warmth in through desert nights that drop close to freezing.

wonder: The smallest fox in the desert was given the biggest ears — and everything else it needed to live where nothing drinks.

name: Three-toed sloth
blurb: A shaggy, slow-moving leaf-eater of Central and South American rainforests that spends almost its entire life hanging upside down in the canopy.
size: About the size of a large house cat, but with much longer arms.

facts.text: Top speed on the ground is about 0.15 mph (0.24 km/h). That is roughly 13 feet (4 m) in a minute. You cover that in two seconds.
facts.more: Slowness is the whole strategy. Leaves carry very little energy, so a sloth spends almost none. It has far less muscle than other mammals its size, and simply cannot move fast, not even to escape.

facts.text: Its arms are much longer than its legs, and each hand ends in three curved claws about as long as your finger.
facts.more: A sloth is built for hanging, not standing. Those long arms reach across gaps between branches without the animal ever having to let go, and the claws do the gripping, so a sloth can hang there and fall asleep.

facts.text: It can take about a month for a single leaf to pass all the way through a sloth. That is the slowest digestion measured in any mammal.
facts.more: Leaves are tough, low in energy and often mildly poisonous. A sloth's four-chambered stomach is packed with microbes that ferment them for weeks. The contents alone can make up a third of the animal's body weight.

facts.text: A sloth climbs all the way down to the forest floor to poop, about once a week. It is the most dangerous thing it ever does.
facts.more: On the ground a sloth is nearly helpless, and many sloths that get eaten are caught on this trip. It digs a small hole at the base of a tree, goes, covers it over, then hauls itself back up.

facts.text: You have seven neck bones. A giraffe has seven. A three-toed sloth has nine, and can swivel its head around roughly 270 degrees.
facts.more: Extra neck bones let a sloth scan for harpy eagles and snakes without moving its body, and a motionless sloth is a nearly invisible sloth. It can also reach leaves all around it without shifting its grip.

facts.text: Sloth fur is grooved, and green algae takes root in the grooves. In the wet season a sloth slowly turns the color of the tree it is sitting in.
facts.more: Each hair is cracked along its length, trapping rainwater for the algae to live in. Beetles, moths and other small creatures move in as well. One sloth can carry a whole miniature community around on its back.

facts.text: A sloth's hair grows the wrong way, from belly toward back, so rain runs straight off a body that spends its life upside down.
Sloths swim about three times faster than they move on the ground. They cross rainforest rivers with a steady doggy-paddle, using the same long arms they hang by.
facts.more: Rivers cut sloth territory into pieces, so crossings matter. In water those arms finally pay off. On land they are useless for walking, and a sloth caught on the ground has to drag itself along by its claws.

facts.text: Wild sloths sleep about 10 hours a day, not the 20 you may have heard. The bigger number came from sloths kept in cages.
facts.more: Researchers fitted wild sloths in Panama with tiny brain-activity recorders and measured 9.6 hours of sleep a day. Captive sloths, with nothing to do and nothing to watch for, slept roughly six hours longer than that.

facts.text: A sloth's eyesight is genuinely poor and its hearing is not much better. It works out which leaves to eat mostly by smell and by touch.
A baby sloth rides on its mother's belly for months, learning which leaves are safe by taking chewed pieces straight from her lips.
facts.more: A poisonous mistake is expensive, so a youngster copies its mother rather than experimenting. It ends up feeding from the same handful of tree species she used, which is why two neighbouring sloths can eat quite different menus.

facts.text: A sloth's body temperature drifts up and down with the weather. On a cool morning it climbs to a sunny branch and warms itself, the way a lizard does.

wonder: Hooked claws, grooved fur, a stomach in no hurry whatsoever. Not everything was made to be fast.

name: Naked mole-rat
blurb: A nearly hairless, buck-toothed rodent from East Africa that spends its whole life underground in a colony organized like an ant nest.
size: About as long as your finger, and about as heavy as a large strawberry.

facts.text: A colony has one queen. Only she has babies. Everyone else digs, cleans, feeds and defends. Ants and bees live like this. Almost no mammals do.
facts.more: Colonies average 75 to 80 animals, and nests of more than 300 have been found. The queen shoves and head-butts the workers, and that pressure keeps the rest of the colony from breeding. When she dies, several females fight for the job.

facts.text: It is about as long as your finger and weighs around 35 grams, the same as a large strawberry. The queen is the only one who outgrows that.
facts.more: A queen passes 50 grams easily and the largest on record reached 80. Everything else about the body is built for tunnels: a tube shape, loose wrinkly skin it can twist around inside, almost no fur, and eyes so small they are hard to find.

facts.text: Its front teeth sit outside its lips. It can seal its mouth shut behind them, which means it can dig with its teeth without swallowing soil.
facts.more: About a quarter of a naked mole-rat's muscle is jaw muscle. You use roughly one per cent of yours on chewing. Each of the four front teeth also moves on its own, so the animal can work them like a pair of chopsticks.

facts.text: Take the air away completely and a naked mole-rat carries on for about 18 minutes. A mouse in the same sealed jar dies in under a minute.
facts.more: With no oxygen, its brain and heart switch to burning fructose, a sugar no other mammal can use for fuel this way. The animal slows almost to a stop, then starts up again when air returns. Crowded burrows get stuffy, and this is how it copes.

facts.text: It is the only mammal that barely warms itself. A naked mole-rat's body temperature just matches its tunnel, so it huddles in heaps or shifts to a warmer level.
facts.more: Most mammals burn food constantly to hold one steady temperature. A naked mole-rat does not bother, which saves an enormous amount of energy. When it gets cold, the colony stacks up into a pile of bodies, or moves up to shallower soil warmed by the sun.

facts.text: Chilli pepper does nothing to a naked mole-rat. Acid does not sting it either. Its skin nerves simply do not send that message to its brain.
facts.more: Burrow air is thick with carbon dioxide, which turns skin acidic and would leave any other mammal in constant discomfort. Naked mole-rats lack the chemical messenger that carries that particular signal, so life down there does not hurt. Pain researchers study them closely.

facts.text: A mouse this size lives about three years. Naked mole-rats have passed 30, and the oldest on record was over 37.
facts.more: Stranger still, their chance of dying in a given year barely climbs as they get older, which is not how ageing usually works. They also very rarely develop cancer. That combination is why laboratories all over the world keep colonies of them.

facts.text: One colony's tunnels can add up to 2 or 3 miles (3 to 5 km) of corridor, dug by animals the length of your finger, mostly with their teeth.
facts.more: They dig in a chain. The animal at the front chisels away at the soil face, and the ones behind sweep the loose dirt backwards with their feet, passing it down the line until someone at the end kicks it out of a hole at the surface.

facts.text: A naked mole-rat runs backwards exactly as fast as it runs forwards. In a tunnel with no room to turn around, that is the only sensible design.
facts.more: Fine hairs scattered over its otherwise bare skin tell it where the tunnel walls are, and its short tail works as a feeler behind it. Its eyes are tiny and nearly useless down there, so touch and smell do all the work.

facts.text: When a female becomes queen, her body gets longer. The gaps between her backbones stretch open to make room for the pups she will carry.
facts.more: That is odd, because she is already a fully grown adult and most mammals stop growing there. A litter of eleven or twelve pups is perfectly ordinary. Workers take over the pups almost as soon as they can walk.

facts.text: Pups beg the queen for her droppings and eat them. It sounds revolting. It is how they pick up the gut microbes they need to digest tough roots.
facts.more: Naked mole-rats live on underground tubers, which are almost impossible to break down without help from the right bacteria. Those bacteria have to come from somewhere. Rabbits and several other plant-eaters do their own version of the same thing.

facts.text: They eat a root from the inside out, hollowing it into a shell but leaving the skin intact, so the plant survives and quietly refills the larder.

wonder: Blind, bare and buried in the dark, and fitted out for every single thing that dark throws at it.

name: Pangolin
blurb: The only mammal covered head to tail in hard scales, a shy night-time insect eater that curls into an armoured ball when it is frightened.
size: Body about as long as your arm, with a tail just as long again.

facts.text: Every scale is keratin, the same material as your fingernails. A pangolin is wearing several hundred overlapping fingernails, and they make up roughly a fifth of its weight.
facts.more: The scales lie over each other like roof tiles and have edges sharp enough to cut. They keep growing and wear down as the animal digs and squeezes through burrows, exactly the way your nails do. A newborn's scales are pale and soft, and harden within days.

facts.text: Pangolins come in wildly different sizes. The smallest weighs about as much as a pet rabbit. The giant pangolin is as heavy as a Labrador.
facts.more: The long-tailed pangolin is around 2 to 2.5 kg (5 lb) and lives up in the trees. The giant pangolin stays on the ground and can reach roughly 33 kg (73 lb). Same armor, same tongue, same trick of rolling up, on completely different scales.

facts.text: Threatened, a pangolin rolls into a ball so tight that a big cat cannot get in. Predators have been filmed batting one around and eventually giving up.
facts.more: Its name comes from a Malay word meaning one who rolls up. Curled up, the tail locks over the head and only scale edges face outward. It can also lash out with that tail. This works beautifully against a leopard, and not at all against a human hand, which is the pangolin's tragedy.

facts.text: The biggest pangolins can push a tongue 16 inches (40 cm) out of their mouths, and it is barely half a centimeter thick. It is not anchored in the mouth at all.
facts.more: The root of the tongue sits deep in the chest near the breastbone, not up in the jaw like yours. When it is not in use it slides back into a sheath in there. Sticky saliva coats the whole length, so ants and termites simply stick and come back with it.

facts.text: No teeth. None at all. A pangolin still puts away 5 to 7 ounces (140-200 g) of ants and termites in a day, without chewing a single one.
facts.more: Instead of teeth it has a muscular stomach lined with hard keratin spines, and it swallows small stones on purpose. Stomach, stones and spines grind the insects up together. A chicken's gizzard works on exactly the same principle.

facts.text: When it tears open a termite mound, a pangolin can close its nostrils and ears and shut a set of thick eyelids. Nothing angry gets in while it eats.
Cornered, a pangolin can spray a foul-smelling liquid from a gland under its tail. Skunks are famous for this trick. Pangolins do it without the publicity.
A pangolin pup rides on the base of its mother's tail. If she is alarmed and rolls up, the baby is folded away inside the ball with her.
facts.more: The pup is born with soft scales and stays pressed against its mother in a burrow for the first weeks. It rides along for around three months, which is also how it learns which mounds are worth ripping open.

facts.text: A pangolin walks on its knuckles with the front claws tucked under, keeping the digging edges sharp. Some species walk almost upright, tail out behind as a counterweight.
The long-tailed pangolin has 49 tail bones, more than any other mammal, and can hang its entire body weight from that tail.
facts.more: All those joints make the tail grippy along its whole length, so it works like a fifth limb in the trees. The animal can dangle upside down from a branch with every foot free for digging into a nest.

facts.text: A pangolin sees badly and hunts almost entirely by nose. It can smell an ant colony through solid ground and dig straight down onto it.
The pangolin is the most trafficked wild mammal on Earth. More than a million were taken from the wild in a single decade, for scales that are only fingernail.
facts.more: Every pangolin species is now protected and international trade in them is banned. Rangers, sniffer dogs and rescue centers work on pangolins full time. Hardly any child has ever seen one in the wild, which is exactly why they are worth knowing about.

wonder: Armour plate, a tongue rooted in the chest, a stomach full of stones. One small animal, kitted out completely for a life of eating ants.

name: Platypus
blurb: An Australian river mammal with a soft duck-like bill, webbed feet and a beaver's tail, and one of only five kinds of mammal in the world that lay eggs.
size: About as long as your arm from elbow to fingertips, and smaller than most people picture.

facts.text: A platypus hunts with its eyes, ears and nostrils all shut. Its bill carries about 40,000 sensors that pick up the faint electricity of a shrimp's twitching muscles.
facts.more: This is electroreception. Every muscle movement leaks a tiny electric field into the water. Packed in beside them are tens of thousands of touch sensors, and together they build a picture of a muddy riverbed the platypus never actually sees. It sweeps its head side to side as it swims, scanning.

facts.text: A platypus lays eggs. Usually two, each about as wide as a grape and soft like leather, and the mother curls around them in a burrow for roughly ten days.
facts.more: The young hatch blind, bald and about the size of a jellybean. They stay underground for three or four months before they ever see the river, by which time they are close to full grown.

facts.text: Platypus mothers have no nipples. Milk seeps out through the skin of the belly, pools in grooves in the fur, and the babies lap it up from there.
Male platypuses have a spur on each back ankle that delivers venom. It will not kill you, but people who have been spurred describe pain that morphine barely touches.
facts.more: Only the males have working spurs, and the venom runs strongest in the breeding season, which points at fights with other males rather than defense. There is no antivenom. Human victims have reported the hand aching for weeks, sometimes months, afterwards.

facts.text: Males are noticeably bigger than females: about 20 inches (50 cm) nose to tail-tip against 17 inches (43 cm), and close to twice the weight.
facts.more: A big male is around 1.7 kg (nearly 4 lb) and a female around 0.9 kg (2 lb). Almost everyone imagines a platypus far larger than it really is. Held in two hands, it is about the bulk of a small cat.

facts.text: A platypus has no working stomach. Its gullet runs almost straight into its intestine, with no acid bag in between at all.
facts.more: It has no adult teeth either. It scoops food into cheek pouches, surfaces, and grinds the lot between rough horny pads in its jaws. Young platypuses do grow small teeth, but they fall out early and never come back.

facts.text: Shine an ultraviolet light on a platypus and its plain brown fur glows cyan and green. Researchers noticed it on museum specimens, then found it on living animals too.
The front feet are the paddles. The webbing folds away under the palm when the platypus walks on land, so the claws can take over for digging.
facts.more: Underwater the web spreads out well past the claws and the animal rows with its front feet, steering with the back feet and tail. On land it walks on its knuckles with the web tucked back, which is why a platypus on a riverbank looks so awkward.

facts.text: That flat tail is not a paddle. It is a pantry. A platypus stores much of its fat reserve in its tail, and a well-fed one has a noticeably fat tail.
You have two sex chromosomes. A platypus has ten.
facts.more: In nearly every other mammal, sex comes down to a single pair, X and Y. A male platypus carries five X and five Y chromosomes, which link up in a chain when its cells divide. No other group of mammals does it this way.

facts.text: A nesting mother digs a burrow into the riverbank that can run 100 feet (30 m) back, then plugs it behind her with packed soil.
facts.more: The plugs keep the temperature and humidity steady inside and keep snakes and goannas out. She has to break through her own wall every time she leaves to feed, and rebuild it when she returns.

facts.text: One dive lasts about 35 seconds. A platypus hunting through the night may make well over a thousand of them, and eat around a fifth of its own body weight.
facts.more: It works mostly at night along the river bottom, taking insect larvae, worms and small freshwater shrimp. Each dive is a quick sweep of the bill through the silt, then back to the surface to chew and breathe before going down again.

wonder: A bill that reads electricity, fur that glows, eggs, venom, and milk that arrives like sweat. Some things were clearly made without a category in mind.

name: Echidna
blurb: A spine-covered, ant-eating Australian mammal that lays a single egg into a pouch on its own belly, and one of only five kinds of egg-laying mammal in the world.
size: About the size of a rugby ball, or a curled-up cat wearing spines.

facts.text: An echidna lays one leathery egg straight into a pouch on her belly. Ten days later a baby hatches inside the pouch, about the size of a jellybean.
facts.more: The hatchling is called a puggle. It weighs about a third of a gram, lighter than a raisin, and is blind, hairless and pink. There is no nipple to find: milk comes out of a patch of skin and the puggle laps it up. It stays in the pouch two to three months.

facts.text: The pouch is not permanent. It is a fold of muscle the mother tightens into a pocket only when she has an egg, and lets go of afterwards.
An echidna's beak reads electricity. Around 400 tiny sensors in the skin pick up the faint electric flicker of termites moving through damp soil.
facts.more: A platypus has about a hundred times more of these sensors, because water carries electricity far better than dirt does. An echidna's work best when the ground is wet, which is one reason echidnas get busy after rain.

facts.text: Frightened, an echidna does not run. It digs straight down where it stands, sinking until nothing shows but a shield of spines.
facts.more: Its legs are short and startlingly strong. On soft ground it can disappear in under a minute, and once wedged into a crevice it cannot be pulled out by a person. The spines are not quills but modified hairs, up to 2 inches (5 cm) long.

facts.text: An echidna has no teeth. It grinds ants and termites between hard pads at the base of its tongue and the roof of its mouth, then swallows the paste.
facts.more: The tongue is long, thin and coated in sticky saliva, and it flicks in and out of a mound faster than you can follow. A feeding echidna also swallows a lot of soil, which helps with the grinding.

facts.text: An echidna runs cooler than nearly every other mammal, about 86-90°F (30-32°C). Put your hand on one and it feels less warm than a dog.
facts.more: It can let that temperature fall much further. Echidnas go into torpor and full hibernation, cooling toward the soil around them, with the heart slowing to four to seven beats a minute. Yours is beating around eighty right now.

facts.text: Echidnas survive bushfires by going underground and shutting down. Researchers tracking them have found animals alive in burned country where almost nothing else made it.
facts.more: They shelter in burrows, logs and rock crevices and drop into torpor, which lowers how much oxygen and energy they need. They can hold that state for up to three weeks. Afterwards they come out into a landscape full of insects and very few competitors.

facts.text: An echidna's back feet point backwards, and one claw on each is extra long. That claw is a comb, and it is the only way to scratch through a coat of spines.
In breeding season, as many as ten males will line up nose to tail behind one female and follow her for weeks. It is called a train.
facts.more: The train can trail her for up to four weeks, with males dropping out and new ones joining on the end. When she finally stops, the males dig a trench in a ring around her and shove each other out of it.

facts.text: Echidnas live across more of Australia than any other native mammal: snowy mountains, bare desert, wet forest, the edges of cities. Very few animals cope with a spread like that.
Echidnas can swim. They paddle along with only the tip of the beak above the surface, using it as a snorkel, and have been watched crossing rivers.
facts.more: The spines trap air and the short legs paddle well enough, so an echidna in water is far less clumsy than an echidna on a road. They have been recorded swimming in the sea as well as in rivers and dams.

facts.text: An echidna curls up to about the size of a rugby ball, and weighs anywhere from 4 to 15 pounds (2-7 kg) depending on where in Australia it lives.
facts.more: Tasmanian echidnas are the biggest and by far the furriest, with thick hair pushing up between the spines. Desert echidnas are smaller with barely any fur at all. Most wild echidnas live around ten years, though individuals have reached forty.

wonder: It lays an egg, senses electricity, and waits out a fire underground. One small spiny animal holding an armful of surprises.

name: Bottlenose dolphin
blurb: A fast, clever sea mammal that breathes air, travels in groups, and hunts fish by firing sound into the water and listening to what comes back.
size: About as long as a small car — most adults run 2 to 4 m (6.5 to 13 ft) from nose to tail.

facts.text: Click. Listen. Click again. A dolphin fires sound out of its forehead and reads the echoes coming back — echolocation — until it knows a fish's size, shape and direction without ever seeing it.
facts.more: The clicks are made in air passages under the blowhole and focused through a fatty lump in the forehead called the melon. Echoes return through the lower jawbone to the ear. In tests, dolphins picked out a target the size of a tennis ball from more than 100 m away — the length of a football field.

facts.text: A dolphin never fully falls asleep. Half its brain rests while the other half keeps watch and remembers to breathe — because for a dolphin, breathing is a decision, not a reflex.
facts.more: Blacking out underwater would be fatal, so the two halves of the brain take turns and then swap over. In one study, dolphins kept echolocating and reporting targets accurately for five days straight, without the sloppy mistakes a sleep-starved human would make.

facts.text: Every dolphin invents its own whistle in its first months and keeps it for life. Other dolphins copy that exact whistle to call it over — the nearest thing to a name in the ocean.
facts.more: Researchers can identify individual wild dolphins by whistle alone. When a mother and calf get separated in murky water, they trade each other's signature whistles back and forth until they meet up again.

facts.text: A dolphin cannot smell anything at all — it has no olfactory nerves, and no smelling lobe in the brain either. It hears astonishingly well instead, and reads the whole water column with sound.
In Florida's shallow bays, one dolphin swims a fast tight circle, beating its tail to kick up a ring of mud. The trapped fish panic, leap, and land in the mouths waiting outside.
facts.more: It is called mud-ring feeding and it needs a cast: one ring-maker, several catchers holding position. Not every dolphin population does it. The trick runs in particular family groups, so dolphins a bay away may never have seen it done.

facts.text: Some dolphins in Shark Bay, Australia, tear a cone-shaped sponge off the seafloor and wear it over the snout like a glove while poking through sharp rubble for hidden fish.
facts.more: The sponge guards the beak from scrapes and stings. Calves learn it by swimming beside their mothers and start carrying their own small sponge while still young. It is the best-documented case of tool use in a sea mammal.

facts.text: Count the teeth and you get somewhere between 72 and 112, every one the same simple cone. They are for gripping, not chewing — a dolphin swallows its fish whole, head first.
A dolphin calf is born tail first and has to reach the surface for its first breath within seconds. Its mother nudges it up. Then it rides in her slipstream for years.
facts.more: Calves nurse for around eighteen months to two years and often stay with their mother for three to six. A dolphin has no lips to suck with, so the mother squirts milk into the calf's mouth using muscle around the mammary gland.

facts.text: Top speed is about 18 mph (29 km/h) — faster than any human has ever swum — but only in short bursts. Cruising, a dolphin ambles along at roughly walking pace.
At speed a dolphin leaps clear of the water again and again. Air is thinner than water to push through, so porpoising like that is cheaper than staying under.
facts.more: Dolphins also ride the pressure wave shoved ahead of a boat or a big whale, coasting along on someone else's effort without a single beat of the tail. Bow-riding dolphins can hold station there for a long time and barely work at all.

facts.text: That hole on top of the head is its nostril, sealed by a muscular flap the dolphin opens on purpose. Underwater the flap stays shut. Not a drop gets in.
A bottlenose dolphin's brain is bigger than yours — about 1.6 kg (3.5 lb) against a human's 1.4 kg. Brain size on its own does not measure cleverness, but that is a lot of brain.

wonder: Half a brain resting, half on watch, night after night for a whole lifetime — a design that never has to stop breathing in order to rest.

name: Sea otter
blurb: A dog-sized sea mammal of the cold North Pacific that floats on its back, cracks shellfish open on its own chest, and wears the thickest fur coat of any animal.
size: About as long as a nine-year-old is tall — up to 1.5 m (5 ft) from nose to tail tip.

facts.text: No blubber. None at all. Instead, up to a million hairs packed into a patch of skin the size of a postage stamp — the densest fur of any animal on Earth.
facts.more: The fur works by trapping a layer of air right against the skin, so an otter is really wearing a coat of bubbles. That is why otters groom constantly: fur that gets dirty or oiled lets the air out, and a soaked otter cannot warm itself up again.

facts.text: A sea otter eats at least a quarter of its own body weight every single day. Scaled to you, that would be roughly 8 kg (18 lb) of food — around 80 apples — before bedtime.
facts.more: Staying warm in near-freezing water burns enormous energy, and the otter has no fat layer to fall back on. Its body burns fuel two to three times faster than a land mammal of the same size, so it dives and eats almost all day: urchins, crabs, clams, snails, mussels.

facts.text: Under each front leg is a loose pocket of skin. The otter stuffs it with food it has collected — and often with one favorite rock, carried up and down between dives.
facts.more: Floating on its back, the otter sets the rock on its chest and hammers shellfish against it until they crack. Some individuals keep the same stone for a long stretch. Sea otters are among the very few mammals anywhere known to use tools.

facts.text: It hunts mostly by feel. Down on a dark, murky seafloor the otter sweeps sensitive paws and whiskers through loose rock and kelp instead of looking for its dinner.
facts.more: In laboratory tests, sea otters told rough surfaces from smooth faster than humans could, and were just as accurate using their whiskers as their paws. Where the light is bad and the water is stirred up, touch simply beats sight.

facts.text: Otters sleep floating, and they hate to drift. They wrap themselves in strands of kelp like a seatbelt, or hold paws with the otter beside them. A group of them is called a raft.
facts.more: Rafts range from a few animals to dozens, with males and females usually resting in separate groups. Holding paws also lifts those bare pads clear of the water — paw pads are one of the few places on an otter with no fur to keep the heat in.

facts.text: A newborn pup is so fluffy it physically cannot sink. It bobs on the surface like a cork while its mother dives, and it cannot follow her under for weeks.
facts.more: The baby coat holds so much air that diving is impossible. A mother often parks her pup wrapped in kelp so it will not drift off, and grooms it for hours every day. A pup that is not groomed gets wet to the skin, and a wet pup gets dangerously cold.

facts.text: A pup left alone on the surface screams — a thin, gull-like cry that carries a long way over open water — and keeps screaming until its mother's head pops up.
Eat enough purple sea urchins and it shows. The pigment from the urchins soaks into the otter, and its teeth and bones can end up stained purple.
Where otters hunt, kelp forests stand. Otters eat sea urchins, and urchins chew through the kelp's anchors. Remove the otters and the urchins mow the forest down to bare rock.
facts.more: Divers call that stripped rock an urchin barren. Surveys in Monterey Bay found kelp holding on in exactly the patches where otters were feeding hardest — one animal's appetite propping up an entire underwater forest.

facts.text: Engineers have built rubbery, hairy materials modelled on otter and beaver fur that hold a layer of air underwater — a possible route to a warmer, lighter kind of wetsuit.

wonder: No blubber, no fire, no shelter — just a coat made so finely that a trapped skin of air keeps a warm animal alive in freezing water.

name: Walrus
blurb: An enormous Arctic sea mammal with two ivory tusks and a bristling mustache, built for hauling out on sea ice and vacuuming clams off the seafloor.
size: Heavier than a small car — a big male can pass 1,200 kg (2,600 lb) and stretch over 3 m (10 ft).

facts.text: Those tusks are teeth — two upper canines that never stop growing. On a big male they reach about 1 m (3 ft), roughly the length of a baseball bat.
facts.more: Walruses hook them into the ice to drag themselves out of the water, which is where the genus name Odobenus, 'tooth-walker', comes from. They also chip breathing holes with them, and males square off and display them. The bigger set usually wins without a fight.

facts.text: Count the whiskers: 400 to 700 of them, in thirteen to fifteen neat rows across the snout. In pitch-black water a walrus finds clams buried in mud entirely by feel.
facts.more: Each whisker is a vibrissa, rooted in its own bed of muscle, blood and nerve, and swept across the seafloor like fingers reading a page. Walruses feed far below the reach of light. Touch is not a backup sense for them — it is the entire hunt.

facts.text: A walrus does not chew a clam. It clamps its lips over the shell and yanks its thick tongue back like a piston, and the suction rips the animal straight out.
facts.more: The empty shells drop back to the seafloor and only the soft body goes down. A single walrus can take several thousand clams in one feeding bout, and it works over snails, worms and sea cucumbers on the same trip.

facts.text: A walrus can sleep in open water without drowning. It inflates two air sacs in its throat like built-in water wings and bobs there, head up, fast asleep.
facts.more: The pouches are pockets off the windpipe that hold many liters of air. Males use them for something else too: a deep, bell-like note produced underwater that carries far enough to be heard through the hull of a boat.

facts.text: A walrus changes color. After a long, cold dive its skin looks pale, almost white. Warm up in the sun on a beach and it flushes pink all over.
facts.more: In cold water the blood vessels near the surface clamp down to hold heat in the core, which drains the color out of the skin. On land they open wide again to dump heat. A pink walrus is a walrus letting off steam.

facts.text: Walruses pile onto ice and beaches in their thousands, body pressed against body. It is warm and it is safe, but the herd spooks easily, and a stampede crushes the animals underneath.
facts.more: A haul-out can hold tens of thousands of animals shoulder to shoulder, and it is a loud place: grunts, roars, and the clatter of tusks on tusks. Young walruses often just climb up and rest on top of the adults rather than fight for floor space.

facts.text: A walrus calf is born already the weight of a grown man — 45 to 75 kg (100 to 165 lb) — and stays with its mother for two years or more.
facts.more: That is among the longest and strongest mother-and-baby bonds of any seal, sea lion or walrus. Mothers carry small calves on their backs in the water and defend them hard. A calf drinks milk for over a year while it learns where the clam beds are.

facts.text: Under that wrinkled hide sits a blubber layer up to 15 cm (6 in) deep — about the length of your hand — and it is the only thing between a warm animal and near-freezing water.
An old male's neck and shoulders are armoured in thick, knobbly lumps of skin called bosses. In a shoving match, they blunt the point of another walrus's tusks.
Males sing under the ice. A courting walrus works through a long pattern of knocks, taps, whistles and that deep gonging bell, and repeats it for hours on end.
Feeding dives usually last five to ten minutes in water shallower than 80 m (260 ft) — about as deep as a 25-story building is tall. A walrus goes where the clams are.

wonder: Whiskers that read the dark, a tongue that pulls like a pump, and a throat that turns into a life jacket — every piece of a walrus is fitted to a sea with no light in it.

name: Star-nosed mole
blurb: A small, dark, mud-loving mole with twenty-two pink tentacles ringing its nose — and the fastest eater ever measured among mammals.
size: Palm-sized — about 20 cm (8 in) from nose to tail tip, and roughly the weight of a golf ball.

facts.text: Twenty-two pink tentacles ring its nose, and not one of them is for smelling. They are for touching. The star carries more than 100,000 nerve fibers — about six times what your entire hand has.
facts.more: The touch sensors are called Eimer's organs, and about 25,000 of them cover a star only 1 cm across — less than the width of your fingernail. The mole flicks it from spot to spot roughly a dozen times a second, building a picture of the tunnel by feel alone.

facts.text: Fastest eater on record. From first touch to swallowed, a star-nosed mole handles a worm in about a quarter of a second — and at its very quickest, barely a tenth.
facts.more: Its brain takes roughly 8 milliseconds to decide whether something is food — close to the physical speed limit of a nerve signal. Researchers needed high-speed video just to see it happen. To your eye, the mole twitches and the worm is simply gone.

facts.text: It can smell underwater. The mole puffs a bubble of air out of its nostrils onto something on the streambed, then sucks the same bubble straight back in and reads the scent it collected.
facts.more: It blows eight to twelve tiny bubbles a second — the same rhythm a mouse sniffs with on land. Only the star-nosed mole and a couple of water shrews are known to manage it. In tests, moles followed underwater scent trails to a worm with near-perfect accuracy.

facts.text: Its eyes are the size of a pinhead and barely work. In a black tunnel there is nothing to look at anyway, so the star does the seeing instead.
Other moles want dry ground. This one wants mud. It tunnels through soggy meadows, marshes and stream banks, and plenty of its tunnels open straight out into the water.
It swims well, and it does not stop for winter. Star-nosed moles have been watched paddling beneath the ice of frozen streams and tunnelling their way through snow.
Its front feet are turned permanently outwards like a pair of shovels, and they are nearly as wide as they are long — made for shifting soil sideways, not for walking.
Dinner is worms, insect larvae and small water creatures, most of them smaller than a grain of rice. Because it handles each one so fast, tiny prey is still worth catching.
facts.more: A slower animal would burn more energy chasing a speck of food than the speck is worth, so it ignores them. The star-nosed mole eats a very large number of very small animals, and the speed of its star is what makes that a living.

facts.text: One litter a year, usually four or five pups, raised in a nest of dry grass built above the waterline. A newborn weighs about as much as a paperclip, and its star is folded flat.
Almost everything eats it. Owls and hawks take them at the surface, skunks dig them out, and large fish snap them up while they are swimming.

wonder: Twenty-two tentacles, a hundred thousand nerve fibers, and a decision made in eight thousandths of a second — all packed into an animal the size of a golf ball.

name: Capybara
blurb: The largest rodent in the world — a calm, barrel-shaped, grass-eating animal of South America that lives with one foot in the river.
size: About the size of a big dog but built like a barrel — up to 1.3 m (4 ft) long, and heavier than most nine-year-olds.

facts.text: It is a rodent, in the same great group as mice and squirrels, and it can outweigh you. A large capybara passes 60 kg (130 lb) and stands about knee-high to an adult.
Its front teeth never stop growing, and neither do its back ones. It grinds them down all day on tough grass — a mouth that wears out and rebuilds itself at the same time.
facts.more: That is the deal every rodent lives by: ever-growing incisors that must be worn down or they overgrow. The capybara takes it further than most, because grass is full of grit and silica, and the back teeth grind constantly too.

facts.text: Look at the head. Eyes, ears and nostrils all sit high on the skull in one line, so the capybara can float with its whole body hidden and still see, hear and breathe.
Trouble on the bank? The capybara walks into the river and vanishes. It can hold its breath for up to five minutes, and surfaces with nothing showing but two nostrils.
facts.more: Its feet are partly webbed, so it swims strongly rather than splashing about, and it can doze in the shallows with only its nose above water. Jaguars, caimans and anacondas all hunt capybaras. The river is the escape route, every time.

facts.text: A capybara eats grass. That is very nearly the whole menu — grass, water plants, some bark and fruit — several kilos of it a day, cropped short with those chisel teeth.
Grass is hard to unlock, so every morning a capybara eats its own droppings — a special soft kind — and runs the whole meal through its body a second time.
facts.more: Rabbits and hares do exactly the same. The first trip through the gut lets bacteria break the tough fibers apart; the second trip is when the animal actually absorbs what those bacteria made. Skip it and you would starve on a full stomach.

facts.text: Capybaras are chatty. They purr, whistle, click, huff and bark, and a grazing family keeps up an almost constant low churring so nobody wanders off.
facts.more: A sharp bark is the alarm: the whole group freezes, then heads for water. Pups purr steadily while they feed and mothers answer them. In grass taller than a young capybara, sound is how the herd keeps track of itself.

facts.text: Pups arrive ready for work — eyes open, fur on, nibbling grass within about a week. In a big group the youngsters bunch into one crowd, and females will nurse pups that are not their own.
They live in groups of roughly ten to twenty, swelling to fifty or more in the dry season when everyone crowds around the last water. Someone always has their head up while the rest eat.
Birds land on them and they simply do not mind. Caracaras and other birds ride around on a capybara's back picking off ticks — a free meal for the bird, fewer parasites for the capybara.
Barrel body, stumpy legs, and still quick: a capybara can hit around 35 km/h (22 mph) in a short dash — faster than you can run — before it reaches the water and dives.
facts.more: It is a sprinter, not a distance runner. Everything about the escape is short: burst across open ground, hit the river, submerge. On land a capybara is prey. In the water it is a strong swimmer that can hold its breath longer than anything chasing it wants to.

facts.text: A male carries a bare dark lump on top of his snout called a morrillo. He rubs it along plants and grass stems to leave a scent that marks whose stretch of riverbank this is.

wonder: Eyes, ears and nose set in one high line, feet half webbed, teeth that never wear out — a grass-eater fitted exactly to the edge of a river.

name: Giraffe
blurb: The tallest animal alive — a spotted, long-necked browser that eats the treetops nothing else can reach.
size: Tall enough to look in through an upstairs window

facts.text: A big bull stands about 5.5 m (18 ft) tall. Stand him beside a basketball hoop and his head is still more than two meters clear above the rim.
facts.more: Almost all of that is leg and neck. A giraffe's front legs alone are about as tall as a grown-up, and the neck adds nearly two meters on top. Which is why, to drink from a puddle, it has to splay those front legs wide and fold itself down like a deckchair.

facts.text: Your neck has seven bones in it. So does a giraffe's. Just seven — but a single one can be longer than your whole forearm.
facts.more: The bones are stretched, not multiplied. One giraffe neck vertebra can measure over 28 cm (11 in). That is why the neck bends in long smooth curves instead of coiling tightly the way a swan's does.

facts.text: A giraffe's blood pressure is roughly twice yours. It has to be — the heart is pushing blood two meters straight uphill to reach the brain.
facts.more: Doing that needs a very thick-walled left ventricle, the heart's main pumping chamber. And when the head swings down to drink, a mesh of fine vessels at the base of the skull called the rete mirabile soaks up the surge, so the brain never gets flooded.

facts.text: The tongue is dark purple-blue and about 45 cm (18 in) long — long enough to reach in past the thorns and strip an acacia branch bare.
facts.more: It is prehensile, meaning it grips. The giraffe wraps it round a branch and drags the leaves off through its lips, thick saliva coating the thorns on the way down. A giraffe can put away 34 kg (75 lb) of leaves in a day.

facts.text: Giraffes were long thought to be nearly silent. Then researchers left microphones running overnight and caught them humming — a low steady note, around 92 hertz.
facts.more: It took over 900 hours of night recordings, and the hums turned up only after dark. One idea is that it is a contact call for when it is too black to see each other. What it actually means, nobody has proved yet.

facts.text: A giraffe sleeps only about four and a half hours out of twenty-four — not in one long night but in short scraps, usually standing up.
facts.more: Deep dreaming sleep barely happens at all: bouts of roughly a minute, adding up to a few minutes a day, with the head curled right back onto its own hindquarters. Lying down takes time to undo, and a giraffe on the ground is a giraffe that cannot run.

facts.text: A giraffe's kick can kill a lion outright. There is a reason lions mostly go after the calves instead.
facts.more: The hoof is the size of a dinner plate and it swings on a leg two meters long. Giraffes can kick forwards, backwards and sideways. A mother will stand over her calf and turn slowly on the spot, keeping the danger in front of her feet.

facts.text: A giraffe is born while its mother is standing up, so its first experience of the world is a two-meter drop. Most are on their feet within the hour.
facts.more: The umbilical cord snaps in the fall. The calf arrives already about 1.8 m (6 ft) tall — as tall as a grown-up — and can run alongside the herd within a day of being born.

facts.text: No two giraffes wear the same spot pattern. It is as individual as your fingerprints, and researchers identify wild giraffes by photographing their sides.
facts.more: Calves inherit the shape and roundness of their blotches from their mothers, so family lines can look alike. And against dappled shade, that pattern breaks up the outline of an animal the size of a truck.

facts.text: A galloping giraffe reaches about 60 km/h (37 mph). At a walk it paces — both legs on the same side swing forward together, the way a camel walks.
Giraffes chew the cud. Watch a resting one and you can see the lump of half-chewed leaves traveling back up two meters of neck to be ground again.
facts.more: Like a cow, a giraffe has a stomach with several chambers. Food goes down, softens, comes back up as cud and gets rechewed. The lump climbing the neck is one of the strangest things you will ever see at a zoo.

facts.text: Males fight by swinging their necks like clubs, landing the blow with the bony knobs on their heads. The knobs are called ossicones, and old bulls wear the hair right off them.

wonder: Made tall — and given everything tall requires: the pressure to climb the neck, and the mesh at the skull to make the way down safe.

name: Hippopotamus
blurb: A river giant that spends its days sunk in the water and its nights out on land, mowing grass.
size: As heavy as a small car, and about as long as one nose to tail

facts.text: A big bull averages around 1,500 kg (3,300 lb) — a small car — and the heaviest on record pushed past two and a half tonnes. On land, only elephants and rhinos outweigh them.
Hippos are not really swimmers. In deep water they walk and bound along the bottom, shoving off and drifting up again in slow, low-gravity leaps.
facts.more: They are too heavy for their size to float easily, so they use the riverbed like a road. An adult surfaces to breathe about every five or six minutes, and its own weight keeps it down there without any effort at all.

facts.text: Eyes, ears and nostrils sit in one line along the top of the skull, so a hippo can see, hear and breathe with the whole rest of it hidden underwater.
facts.more: When it dives, the nostrils clamp shut and the ears fold closed. Nothing gets in. It is the same trick that lets a calf feed underwater without swallowing half the river.

facts.text: Hippo skin oozes a thick red liquid that people used to call blood sweat. It is neither blood nor sweat. It is sunscreen.
facts.more: Chemists pulled two pigments out of it: hipposudoric acid, which is red, and norhipposudoric acid, which is orange. Both soak up ultraviolet light, and one of them slows the growth of bacteria — sunblock and antiseptic, made by the animal's own skin.

facts.text: A hippo's lower canine teeth reach about 50 cm (20 in) — arm's length — and never stop growing. They sharpen themselves every single time the jaws shut.
facts.more: The lower tusks grind against the uppers with each bite, keeping a chisel edge on them. And a yawning hippo is not sleepy. It is opening its mouth to something past a right angle to show you those teeth. It is a warning.

facts.text: For an animal that size the diet is oddly plain: grass. A hippo crops around 40 kg (88 lb) a night, walking three to five kilometers from the water to find it.
facts.more: They graze with their tough lips, not those tusks — the tusks are weapons, not tools. Hippos take the same route night after night, wearing deep double-grooved trails up the riverbanks that you can still see by day.

facts.text: A sleeping hippo can rise, breathe and sink again without ever waking. The surfacing happens by reflex, the way you swallow without deciding to.
Hippos call underwater as well as above it. A submerged hippo can answer another one without either of them lifting a head clear of the river.
Calves are often born in the water and can nurse underwater — nostrils shut, ears folded — letting go every so often to bob up for air.
Hippos are among the most dangerous large animals in Africa, not because they hunt people but because they defend water. A bull will charge anything standing between him and the deep.
facts.more: They are fiercely territorial in the river and much calmer out of it. Guides in hippo country teach one rule above all the others: never put yourself between a hippo and the water, especially at night when the herd is out grazing.

facts.text: A hippo marks its patch by spinning its short flat tail like a propeller while it dungs, flinging the result over bushes, water and rivals alike.
facts.more: It is not only rude. Enormous amounts of that dung end up in the river, feeding insects and fish and carrying nutrients from the grassland into the water. Hippos fertilise the rivers they live in.

wonder: Skin too delicate for the African sun — and the sunscreen supplied with it, built right into the animal.

name: White rhinoceros
blurb: The second-heaviest animal on land: a grass-mowing giant in thick gray hide, with two horns made of the same stuff as your fingernails.
size: As heavy as two small cars, with a back as high as a tall grown-up

facts.text: Only elephants are heavier on land. A bull white rhino averages 2,000 to 2,300 kg (4,400 to 5,000 lb) — two small cars — standing on legs like tree stumps.
That wide square upper lip is a lawnmower. The white rhino grazes short grass, head down, for roughly half of every day.
facts.more: Its neighbor the black rhino has a pointed, grabby upper lip instead, for pulling leaves and twigs off bushes. Same country, same size, completely different mouths — so the two of them almost never want the same mouthful.

facts.text: The horn is not bone and it is not attached to the skull. It is keratin — the same material as your fingernails and hair — and like a fingernail, it keeps growing.
facts.more: Rangers sometimes cut a rhino's horn off to make the animal worthless to poachers. It grows back, because the living base stays behind, the way your nail regrows from under the cuticle.

facts.text: The front horn is usually around 60 cm (2 ft). The longest ever measured was over 150 cm (5 ft) — taller than the child reading this.
A rhino may not recognize you standing still thirty meters away. Its eyes are poor. Its nose is not — smell is how a rhino knows what is out there.
facts.more: Its hearing is sharp too, and the two ears swivel separately, each tracking a different sound. Stand downwind and stay quiet, and a grazing rhino may never work out that you are there at all.

facts.text: White rhinos share communal dung heaps called middens, and every visitor reads them. The dung says who has been by, how old, male or female, and who owns this ground.
facts.more: Researchers found there is even a seating plan. The territory-owning bull dungs in the middle of the midden; females and younger males use the edges. He also times his own deposit for when the midden is busiest, so the message gets read while it is fresh.

facts.text: Two tonnes of animal, and it can still hit 50 km/h (31 mph). That is faster than the fastest human being who has ever run.
A white rhino calf runs in front of its mother, not behind her. Black rhino calves do the exact opposite and follow.
facts.more: The mother steers from behind with her horn and her bulk, keeping the calf out in open view ahead of her where she can see it. A calf stays with her for two or three years, until the next one arrives.

facts.text: Oxpeckers ride on rhinos, picking ticks off the hide. They also hiss an alarm when a person approaches — and rhinos carrying birds notice people far more reliably.
facts.more: In one study, every rhino with oxpeckers aboard detected an approaching human, while rhinos without birds often walked on unaware. The Swahili name for the oxpecker means, roughly, the rhino's guard.

facts.text: Nobody actually knows why it is called the white rhino. It is gray — precisely the same gray as the black rhino.
facts.more: The popular story is that English speakers misheard a Dutch word meaning wide, describing that square lip. Researchers went hunting for that word in old Dutch and Afrikaans writing about rhinos and could not find it used that way at all. The name is still a mystery.

facts.text: Southern white rhinos were once down to fewer than a hundred animals. Guarded and moved to safe reserves, they came back — there are now more of them than all other rhinos put together.
Look at the tracks: three broad toes on every foot, printing like a fat clover leaf. All that weight rides on a springy pad tucked in behind the toes.

wonder: A horn that wears down against the world and simply keeps growing back — an edge that never runs out.

name: Dromedary camel
blurb: The one-humped camel of hot deserts — an animal built to carry a load across country with no water in sight.
size: About as tall at the hump as a grown-up with one arm raised

facts.text: The hump is not a water tank. It is fat — up to about 36 kg (80 lb) of it — food the camel carries around on its own back.
facts.more: When a camel goes hungry, the hump shrinks and flops over sideways like a half-empty bag. Feed it up and the hump firms and stands tall again. You can read a camel's recent luck straight off the shape of its back.

facts.text: A big male stands around 2 m (6 ft 6 in) at the shoulder before you even count the hump, and weighs about as much as a large horse.
A camel will chew a thorn bush that would shred your hands. The inside of its mouth is lined with tough cone-shaped spikes, called papillae, that grip the thorns and steer them down the throat.
facts.more: The papillae all point backwards, so a mouthful can only travel one way. It means a camel can eat the dry, spiny, salty plants nothing else in the desert will touch — which is exactly the food that is still there when everything else is gone.

facts.text: A thirsty camel can drink more than 100 liters (26 gallons) in about ten minutes — fifty big water bottles, straight down, without stopping.
facts.more: Taking on water that fast would burst the red blood cells of most mammals. A camel's are oval instead of round, and stretchy enough to swell to more than twice their size without splitting. It refills at a rate that would kill a horse, then walks away as if nothing happened.

facts.text: Three eyelids. Two ordinary ones, plus a thin third that sweeps sideways like a windscreen wiper — and it is see-through, so the camel can keep walking with it shut.
facts.more: Add two rows of long lashes and nostrils that squeeze down to slits, and a camel can keep going through a sandstorm that would blind you in seconds. Even the ears are lined with hair to keep the grit out.

facts.text: A camel lets its own body temperature drift from about 34°C to 41°C (93°F to 106°F) across a day, so it does not have to start sweating until things are genuinely hot.
facts.more: Cool night, cool camel; by afternoon it has warmed through like a stone in the sun. Every degree it soaks up instead of sweating away is water it gets to keep. Your body would never permit a swing like that.

facts.text: A camel takes water back out of its own breath. The inside of the nose cools the outgoing air and pulls the moisture from it before it can leave.
facts.more: Overnight the nasal lining dries out and turns hygroscopic — meaning it grabs moisture from passing air — so the camel breathes out air that is not even fully damp. Over a day that adds up to a serious share of the water it would otherwise lose.

facts.text: A camel can lose more than a quarter of its body weight in water and carry on walking. In most mammals, half that loss would be deadly.
Look at the feet. Two broad toes on a wide leathery pad that spreads under the weight like a snowshoe, so the camel presses onto the sand instead of down into it.
Camels do spit, and it is not spit. It is stomach contents, brought up on purpose and thrown at whatever is annoying them. It smells exactly as bad as that sounds.
In the mating season a male blows a pink sac the length of your hand out of the side of his mouth, like a wobbling balloon, and gurgles at his rivals. The sac is called a dulla.
A racing camel holds about 40 km/h (25 mph), but the real trick is endurance: a working camel can cover 80 km (50 miles) in a day, and do it again the next day for a week.
facts.more: That is why camels crossed deserts no horse could cross. Not because they were fast, but because they simply did not have to stop.

wonder: God gave the camel three eyelids, two rows of lashes and nostrils that shut — an entire face made ready for the sandstorm before it came.

name: Reindeer
blurb: The deer of the frozen north — the only one whose females grow antlers, and the only one people have ever herded.
size: About the size of a small pony, standing waist-high to a grown-up

facts.text: Reindeer are not big deer — a bull stands about waist-high to a grown-up. But he is dense with it, up to 150 kg (330 lb), the weight of two adults.
A reindeer's eyes change color with the seasons. Gold in summer. Deep blue through the long winter dark.
facts.more: Behind the retina sits a mirror called the tapetum lucidum. In winter, pressure inside the eyeball squeezes its fibers closer together and the mirror turns blue, bouncing less light straight back out and giving the eye far more chance to catch what little there is. The trade is sharpness: the winter eye sees more, but blurrier.

facts.text: Reindeer see ultraviolet light, which you cannot. Snow throws UV back; lichen, fur and urine soak it up. To a reindeer, the blank white world is covered in dark marks.
facts.more: Wolf fur shows as a dark shape against snow that looks empty to us. So does a patch of lichen worth digging for. Human eyes screen UV out to protect the retina; reindeer eyes let it straight through.

facts.text: Reindeer are the only deer whose females grow antlers — and the females hang onto theirs all winter, long after the males have dropped theirs.
facts.more: A pregnant female uses her antlers as a snow shovel and as a door: she can hold a feeding crater against bigger males who no longer have any headgear to argue with. She sheds hers in spring, around the time her calf is born.

facts.text: Some reindeer cover close to 4,800 km (3,000 miles) in a single year between winter range and calving ground — one of the longest journeys any animal makes on land.
facts.more: Satellite collars showed that the distance does not come from one straight march. It is a whole year of movement: north in spring, south in fall, and endless smaller shuffles in between, chasing food and running from insects.

facts.text: Every step a reindeer takes clicks. A tendon slips over a small bone in the foot, and the sound carries — so a herd in fog or blizzard can hear where it is.
facts.more: The click cannot be switched off; it happens whether the animal wants it or not. Stand in a reindeer barn with your eyes closed and the whole room sounds faintly like popping corn.

facts.text: Winter food is lichen — a crust on rock and ground that almost no other animal can digest. Reindeer carry gut microbes that break it down for them.
facts.more: They smell it through deep snow, then dig a crater with their hooves to reach it. Herders call it reindeer moss, though it is nothing of the kind: a lichen is a fungus and an alga living together as one thing.

facts.text: The hooves change with the season. Soft and spongy in summer for wet tundra, they shrink back in winter to leave a hard sharp rim that bites into ice.
Reindeer hair is hollow. Every strand traps air, which holds the heat in and makes the animal float — so herds swim wide rivers and sea channels without much trouble.
A reindeer calf can outrun you the day after it is born. Within a week it can keep pace with the whole running herd.
The nose does the heating. Air arrives freezing and reaches the lungs at nearly body temperature, warmed on the way by scrolls of paper-thin bone inside the muzzle.
facts.more: Those same scrolls, called turbinates, strip the heat and moisture back out of the breath going the other way. So the reindeer is not throwing warmth and water into the Arctic every time it breathes out.

facts.text: Above the Arctic Circle the sun never sets in summer and never rises in midwinter. Reindeer respond by dropping their daily rhythm altogether, feeding and resting right around the clock.

wonder: Eyes that retune themselves for the polar night — the darkness was accounted for before the reindeer ever walked into it.

name: Blue whale
blurb: The largest animal on Earth — a whale longer than two school buses that lives almost entirely on some of the smallest creatures in the sea.
size: Longer than two school buses parked end to end, and heavier than twenty elephants

facts.text: Its heart is about the size of a golf cart and weighs roughly 400 pounds (180 kg) — the largest heart of any animal alive.
facts.more: That figure comes from a real one. A blue whale washed ashore in Newfoundland, Canada, and a museum team cut the heart out, preserved it, and put it on display. It is still the only blue whale heart preserved anywhere in the world.

facts.text: A newborn blue whale is already longer than a car — about 23 feet (7 m). Drinking its mother's milk, it puts on around 200 pounds (90 kg) every single day.
facts.more: The milk is roughly as thick as toothpaste and enormously fatty, which is how a calf gains the weight of a grown man daily. It nurses for six to eight months and does not stop growing the whole time.

facts.text: It eats krill — shrimp-like animals about as long as your little finger. On a heavy feeding day a big blue whale can swallow several tons of them.
No teeth at all. About 300 fringed plates of baleen hang from each side of its upper jaw, made of keratin — the same stuff as your fingernails — and they strain krill from the water.
One lunge takes in more water than the whale's whole body weighs. It swallows nothing yet: first it squeezes all that water back out through the baleen.
