facts.more: The throat has deep grooves called pleats that unfold like an accordion, so the mouth balloons into an enormous bag. The gulp-and-squeeze takes well under a minute, and the whale may repeat it several times on a single dive.

facts.text: Scientists once suction-cupped a heart monitor onto a wild blue whale. On a deep dive its heart slowed to two beats a minute, then raced to 37 back at the surface.
facts.more: Two beats a minute means nearly thirty seconds of silence between beats. Slowing that far saves oxygen while the whale is down. The tag held on with four suction cups, then fell off and was collected floating on the surface.

facts.text: Its calls sit so low that much of the sound is at the very bottom of what people can hear — a rumble you feel in your chest more than hear.
facts.more: Low sounds travel enormous distances in deep water. Researchers listening on underwater microphones can pick up one blue whale from far off and follow it for days without ever laying eyes on it.

facts.text: Its tongue alone weighs about as much as a full-grown elephant — roughly 3 tons (2,700 kg).
Blue whales swim in every ocean, but they are thinly spread and hard to find. Whaling once brought them close to vanishing; they are protected now, and in some seas their numbers are slowly climbing.
Blue whale droppings come out as a bright orange cloud, colored by the shells of all that krill. It is loaded with iron, and it feeds the tiny drifting plants krill live on.
facts.more: The whale feeds deep and releases waste near the surface, carrying nutrients up into sunlit water where plankton can use them. Researchers scoop the floating clouds into fine nets to work out exactly what the whale has been eating.

facts.text: Its blow is a column of misty breath that shoots up 30 feet (9 m) — as high as a two-story house — and you can smell it from the deck of a boat.

wonder: The biggest heart God ever set beating, in an animal that lives on the smallest food in the sea.

name: Humpback whale
blurb: A barnacle-crusted whale with enormous white flippers, famous for leaping clear of the water and for the long songs the males sing.
size: About as long as a school bus, with flippers longer than a canoe

facts.text: Its flippers are the longest of any animal — up to 16 feet (5 m), about a third of its whole body. Its scientific name, Megaptera, means big wing.
The front edge of a humpback's flipper is lumpy, not smooth. Engineers copied those lumps onto wind turbine blades and fans, because they help a wing grip at steep angles.
facts.more: The lumps are called tubercles. They split the flow into channels and delay the moment a wing stalls and loses its lift. That grip is how a whale as heavy as twenty cars can turn in a tight circle underwater.

facts.text: Several whales dive beneath a school of herring and blow a spiralling curtain of bubbles. The fish will not swim through it. Then the whales rise up the middle, mouths open.
facts.more: It is called bubble-net feeding, and it is learned rather than automatic — only some humpback populations do it, and whales appear to pick it up from one another. In a group they take set roles and lunge together on a signal call.

facts.text: Only the males sing. One song can run from a few minutes to half an hour, he repeats it for hours, and every singing male in that stretch of ocean sings the same version.
facts.more: The song changes slowly through the season and all the singers change with it. Sometimes a brand-new song spreads from one ocean population to the next, until whales thousands of miles apart are singing the newcomer.

facts.text: It eats krill and small schooling fish — herring, capelin, sand lance — taken in enormous mouthfuls. Almost all of a year's eating is packed into the cold feeding months.
Some humpbacks swim more than 5,000 miles (8,000 km) between cold feeding seas and warm calving waters — one of the longest migrations any mammal makes.
facts.more: They feed hard through the cold months, then eat little or nothing in the warm breeding waters, living for months on the blubber they packed on. Mothers make the entire journey while nursing a calf.

facts.text: Humpbacks have been recorded charging at hunting orcas and driving them off — and often the animal being rescued was a seal or a sea lion, not a humpback at all.
facts.more: Researchers gathered more than a hundred of these encounters from all over the world. The humpbacks bellow, slash with their tails, and put their huge flippers between the orcas and the prey. Why they bother is still an open question.

facts.text: The knobs on its head are not barnacles. Each one is a tubercle with a single hair growing out of it, wired to nerves — something like a cat's whisker.
No two tails are alike. The black-and-white pattern under the flukes works like a fingerprint, so researchers photograph it and follow the same individual whale for years.
A humpback weighing 30 tons can throw nearly its whole body out of the water and land with a crash you can hear a long way off.
facts.more: Breaching may knock off clinging hitchhikers, or send a signal other whales can hear underwater, or both. Researchers have found humpbacks breach more often once the wind picks up and the sea turns noisy — which fits the idea that the splash is a way of being heard.

facts.text: It carries acorn barnacles cemented right into its skin — around the chin, the flippers and the tail. They are hitchhikers, not parasites, and their kind rides only on whales.
facts.more: Barnacle larvae drift in the water, settle on the whale's skin and grow a hard shell anchored in place. Riding a whale means a constant flow of food-rich water pushed past them. Goose barnacles often grow on top of the acorn barnacles — hitchhikers on hitchhikers.

facts.text: A mother and her calf whisper. They swap quiet grunts and squeaks that carry only a short way, instead of loud calls that would tell an orca exactly where the calf is.
facts.more: Researchers stuck recording tags on calves and found the calls were extremely faint. The calf stays tucked against its mother's side, and she often keeps her own body between the calf and the open sea.

wonder: Given long white wings, a voice that carries for miles, and a habit of turning back for animals that are not its own.

name: Sperm whale
blurb: The largest toothed animal on Earth — a square-headed hunter that dives into the pitch dark to catch squid.
size: Longer than a school bus, with a head the size of a small van

facts.text: A third of a sperm whale is head. Inside is the spermaceti organ — a great case of waxy oil the whale uses to focus and aim its sound.
facts.more: The case can hold hundreds of gallons of oil. Sound made in the whale's nose passages travels back through the case, bounces off an air sac, and leaves the front of the head as a tight, powerful beam of clicks.

facts.text: It hunts in total darkness half a mile down. A dive usually lasts about 45 minutes, but sperm whales have been recorded past 6,500 feet (2,000 m) and under for more than an hour.
facts.more: On the way down its lungs collapse under the pressure, which is exactly what they are built to do. Oxygen is stored in the blood and muscles instead of the lungs, and its muscle is almost black with the stuff.

facts.text: The loudest sounds any animal makes are sperm whale clicks — sharp cracks that carry for miles underwater and can be heard right through a boat's hull.
It hunts blind. A click goes out, an echo comes back off a squid, and the whale reads the darkness from sound alone. That is echolocation.
facts.more: It scans with slow clicks while searching, then speeds them into a buzz as it closes in — the faster the clicks, the more often the picture updates. Researchers listening in can tell from the buzz alone when a hunt is about to end.

facts.text: It eats squid, mostly — a great many of them, and mostly ones no longer than your arm. Some sperm whales carry round scars left by the suckers of giant squid.
facts.more: Nobody has ever watched a sperm whale fight a giant squid; the evidence is the scars and the beaks. A single stomach can hold thousands of hard squid beaks, which is how researchers work out what the whale has been eating.

facts.text: Its teeth are only in the narrow lower jaw — twenty to twenty-six cone-shaped teeth down each side, up to 8 inches (20 cm) long. They fit into sockets in the upper jaw.
Sperm whales sleep standing up. A whole group will hang vertically near the surface, nose-up and completely still, for ten or fifteen minutes at a time.
facts.more: It was discovered almost by accident when a research boat drifted in among motionless whales and they did not react until the hull touched one. They nap in short bursts and appear to sleep less than almost any other mammal.

facts.text: A calf cannot follow its mother down into the cold dark. So it waits at the surface, and another adult from the family stays up there with it until she returns.
facts.more: Sperm whale families are mothers, daughters and young. Babysitting shifts get shared around, and calves sometimes nurse from females that are not their mother. Males leave the family when they grow up and head for colder water alone.

facts.text: It has the largest brain of any animal — around 17 pounds (8 kg), roughly five times the weight of yours.
Families talk in codas: short rhythms of clicks, like knocking on a door. Different clans use different rhythms, and a calf spends its first years learning its own family's.
facts.more: Clans using different codas can share the same stretch of ocean and still keep to their own kind. Researchers can work out which clan they are listening to from a recording, without ever seeing the whales.

facts.text: Squid beaks are too hard to digest. Now and then they bind into a waxy lump called ambergris, which drifts ashore and is worth a fortune to perfume makers.
facts.more: Fresh ambergris smells terrible. After a long time at sea it hardens into a gray, sweet-smelling lump that was used to make perfume last longer on skin. Pieces found on beaches have sold for staggering sums.

facts.text: Its blowhole sits at the front left of its head, so the spout blows forward and off to one side. Whalers could name the whale from miles away by that crooked, bushy blow.

wonder: A head built as a lens for sound, so an animal can find its way where light has never reached.

name: Narwhal
blurb: An Arctic whale with a long spiral tusk growing straight out of its head — a real animal, not a legend.
size: Body about as long as a car, plus a tusk taller than a doorway

facts.text: The tusk is a tooth — the narwhal's left canine, grown straight out through its upper lip. On a big male it reaches 10 feet (3 m) and weighs over 20 pounds (9 kg).
facts.more: Almost every tusk belongs to a male, though a few females grow one and the odd narwhal grows two. The tooth keeps growing for most of the whale's life. Narwhals have no other working teeth — their mouths are otherwise nearly bare.

facts.text: The tusk is not solid armor. It is porous, threaded with millions of tiny nerve channels, and seawater seeps in through the surface to reach them.
facts.more: Researchers fitted narwhals with heart monitors and washed the tusk with water of different saltiness. The heart rate changed. That is real evidence the tusk is a sense organ, feeling the sea the whale swims through.

facts.text: Every narwhal tusk spirals the same way — counterclockwise. Even on the rare whale that grows two tusks, both turn in that same direction.
It has no chewing teeth, so it never chews. It swims up to a Greenland halibut or an Arctic cod and sucks the fish in whole, like a vacuum.
Drone cameras over the Canadian Arctic have filmed narwhals whacking cod with the tusk — a fast downward flick that stuns the fish just long enough to swallow it.
Few air-breathing animals dive deeper. Through the winter narwhals drop past 2,600 feet (800 m) again and again, and the deepest dives on record go well over a mile down.
facts.more: A deep dive lasts up to about 25 minutes, and a narwhal may make fifteen or more in a day. Much of that happens in winter under the ice — so every dive has to end at a crack or hole it can find again in the dark.

facts.text: It spends the whole winter under thick pack ice, in water as black as night, breathing at cracks and holes it must relocate every time it needs air.
There is no fin on its back — only a low bumpy ridge. A tall fin would catch on the ice it lives beneath.
A calf is born a plain gray. As a narwhal grows it turns blotchy and mottled, and the oldest ones fade to almost pure white.
When orcas arrive, narwhals go quiet and press into shallow water near the shore, or into ice packed too tightly for an orca's tall fin to follow.
Narwhals return to the same summer fjord year after year, and to the same wintering water, following the routes their mothers took before them.
Narwhal tusks were once sold in Europe as unicorn horns. Buyers who had never seen the Arctic paid many times the tusk's weight in gold for them.

wonder: God gave the narwhal a tooth that can feel the sea it swims through.

name: Orca
blurb: The ocean's top hunter — a black-and-white animal that lives in families and teaches its young how to hunt.
size: Longer than a car and a half, with a back fin taller than a grown man

facts.text: Despite the name killer whale, an orca is not a whale at all. It is a dolphin — the biggest one there is. A large male reaches 32 feet (9.8 m).
facts.more: A big male can weigh 11 tons, about the same as two elephants. Males outgrow females by a wide margin, and everything on them runs larger: the flippers, the tail, and above all the towering fin on the back.

facts.text: A grown male's back fin can stand 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, taller than most adults. Every fin is nicked and shaped a little differently, so researchers use them to tell individuals apart.
Orcas live in families led by the oldest female. In some populations a son never leaves his mother — he swims beside her for his entire life.
facts.more: The family group is called a matriline: a grandmother, her daughters, her sons, and her daughters' calves. They hunt, travel and rest together, and a whale that gets separated calls until it finds them again.

facts.text: Each family has its own set of calls — a dialect. A calf learns its mother's calls, and researchers can tell which family is going past simply by listening.
Different orca families eat completely different food. Some eat nothing but salmon. Others hunt seals and never touch a fish. They share the same ocean and do not mix.
facts.more: The differences run deep: separate calls, separate hunting methods, even differently shaped fins. A salmon-eating orca and a seal-hunting orca can pass within sight of each other and behave like total strangers.

facts.text: In Antarctica, orcas line up shoulder to shoulder and charge an ice floe together, making a wave that washes the seal on top of it into the water.
facts.more: They have been filmed doing a practice run first, and even nudging the ice around so the seal ends up on the side they want. If the first wave fails, they line up and go again.

facts.text: Off South Africa, orcas have been filmed opening up great white sharks and eating only the liver — the fattiest part — then leaving the rest of the shark behind.
facts.more: Great white carcasses began washing ashore with a neat wound and no liver. Two particular orcas, known by their bent-over fins, are behind many of them, and the white sharks now clear out of the area entirely when those two show up.

facts.text: It finds prey by echolocation, clicking and reading the echoes. But seal-hunting orcas often go almost silent, because a seal can hear those clicks coming.
facts.more: Fish hear orca clicks poorly, so salmon hunters chatter away constantly. Seals and porpoises hear them very well, so the mammal hunters work in near silence and only start talking again once the hunt is finished.

facts.text: Orcas live in every ocean on Earth, from the edge of the ice to the tropics. Few mammals anywhere are spread more widely.
Older females stop having calves but keep leading. In poor salmon years the grandmother swims out in front, and her grandcalves are the ones most likely to make it through.
facts.more: Researchers followed the same families for many years and found that when a grandmother dies, her grandcalves are far more likely to die in the couple of years afterwards. She knows where the fish are when the fish are hardest to find.

facts.text: In Patagonia, orcas rush right up onto the beach to grab a sea lion, then wriggle backwards into the sea. Mothers spend years teaching the young ones how, starting in safe shallow water.
Nothing hunts a healthy orca. It is an apex predator wherever it lives — and there is no confirmed record of a wild orca ever killing a person.

wonder: The oldest mother is her family's map and memory — the wisest kept, not set aside.
The oldest mother is her family's map and memory — the wisest kept, not set aside.

name: Mandrill
blurb: The biggest monkey in the world: a heavy, ground-walking forest primate with a scarlet-and-blue face you could pick out of a crowd from fifty meters.
size: A big male is about as heavy as a nine-year-old child, walking on four legs

facts.text: The mandrill is the largest monkey on Earth. A big male reaches 30 kg (66 lb) — about what a nine-year-old weighs, carried around on four legs.
facts.more: Males run 19 to 30 kg; females only 10 to 15 kg. Few primates differ that much between the sexes. A male can be more than twice the weight of the female sitting beside him, with long canine teeth she does not have.

facts.text: In Gabon's Lope forest, researchers counted a single mandrill horde of 845 animals — the largest group of wild primates ever recorded, apart from people.
facts.more: They counted from film, frame by frame, because nobody can count that many moving animals by eye. Even an ordinary horde runs into the hundreds. When one crosses the forest floor, the ground itself seems to be moving.

facts.text: A male's scarlet nose stripe and blue cheek ridges brighten as he climbs in rank, and fade when he loses the top spot. Rivals read his color like a scoreboard.
facts.more: Researchers followed the same males for years and found the brightest male is nearly always the alpha. Males compare color before anything else happens, which settles a great many arguments without a single bite being thrown.

facts.text: When a male opens his mouth wide at a rival, that is not a yawn. He is showing off canine teeth up to 4.5 cm (1.8 in) long — about the length of your thumb.
facts.more: Those canines are a weapon and an advertisement at once, and usually the advertisement is enough. A wide-mouthed stare across a clearing ends the disagreement, because every mandrill watching can see exactly what is on offer.

facts.text: A mandrill pulling its lips back to bare every tooth is not angry. That enormous grin is a friendly signal, meaning roughly: no trouble from me.
It packs fruit into stretchy pouches inside its cheeks until its head looks lopsided, carries the load somewhere quieter, then pushes the food back into its mouth with a hand.
facts.more: Cheek pouches are standard equipment for the monkeys of Africa and Asia. They let a mandrill grab far more than it can chew while a fruiting tree is crowded and contested, then walk off and eat the lot in peace.

facts.text: A mandrill has a scent gland in the middle of its chest, and presses it against branches as it travels, leaving a smell-message on the trail behind it.
Mandrills eat mostly fruit and seeds, plus insects turned up by rolling logs over. A big male will also chase down and eat a small animal when the chance appears.
facts.more: They spend the day working the forest floor: flipping leaf litter, cracking hard seeds, stripping fruit trees. Because they swallow seeds whole and then walk for kilometers, they end up planting a good deal of the forest they live in.

facts.text: A horde walks kilometers in a day, following the fruit as different trees ripen. Mandrills spend far more time on the ground than most monkeys ever do.
A newborn mandrill has a black coat and a bare pink face, and spends its first weeks slung underneath its mother, gripping her belly fur while she walks.
Mandrills live in the rainforests of west-central Africa — southern Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and parts of Congo — and nowhere else in the wild.

wonder: A whole language painted onto one face, and every mandrill in the forest can read it.

name: Ring-tailed lemur
blurb: A cat-sized primate from the dry south of Madagascar, known everywhere by the long striped tail it carries straight up like a flag.
size: About the size of a house cat, with a tail longer than the rest of it

facts.text: Body about 40 cm (16 in) long; tail about 60 cm (24 in). The tail is longer than the lemur it belongs to — and it cannot grip a branch at all.
facts.more: Monkeys in South America hang by their tails. No lemur can. This tail is a balance pole for running along branches, and a banner held straight up so a troop can keep track of each other in long grass.

facts.text: Count the rings. A ring-tailed lemur's tail carries around thirteen black bands and a dozen or so white ones, and the very tip always finishes black.
Males settle arguments by smell. A male drags his tail across scent glands on his wrists and shoulders, arcs it over his head and wafts it at his rival. It is called a stink fight.
facts.more: A stink fight can go on for an hour of standing and wafting, and the loser walks away without a scratch on him. The wrist glands produce a complicated mixture of chemicals, and the whole troop can smell how it went.

facts.text: A male also gouges saplings with a horny spur on his wrist, cutting into the bark before he scent-marks it, so the smell soaks in and lasts.
The troop keeps different alarm calls for different dangers. One call for a hawk overhead sends everybody down out of the open; another, for a fossa on the ground, sends everybody up.
facts.more: The fossa is Madagascar's largest predator, a long, muscular, cat-like hunter that climbs as well as any lemur. Getting the call right matters enormously: go up a tree for a hawk and you are exposed, go down for a fossa and you are lunch.

facts.text: The boss of a ring-tailed lemur troop is always a female. She eats first, she decides where the group goes, and fully grown males step out of her way.
facts.more: In most primate groups the biggest male is in charge. Here a female half a male's size can take food straight out of his hands and he lets it go. Males often live at the edge of the troop and move between troops.

facts.text: On a cold morning the whole troop sits upright with legs apart and pale bellies turned to the sun, arms resting on knees, warming up before the day's traveling begins.
In the dry forests where they live, the kily — the tamarind tree — supplies a huge share of everything they eat: its fruit, its leaves and its flowers.
Of all the lemurs, this one spends the most time on the ground, walking on all fours between one patch of trees and the next with its striped tail hoisted.
A newborn rides slung under its mother's belly, then graduates after a few weeks to riding on her back, sitting up like a jockey while she leaps.
Wild ring-tailed lemurs live in one place on Earth: the dry southern end of Madagascar, from spiny scrub and gallery forest up into cold mountain country.

wonder: A tail that grips nothing at all, yet balances, signals and settles fights — not one part of this animal is spare.

name: Tarsier
blurb: A tiny night-hunting primate from the islands of Southeast Asia, with eyes so large they cannot move in their sockets and legs built like springs.
size: Small enough to sit in your cupped hands, with a tail twice as long as its body

facts.text: Each eyeball is about 16 mm across — as big as the tarsier's own brain, sometimes bigger. No mammal has larger eyes for its body size.
facts.more: Scaled up to your size, you would be walking around with eyes as big as grapefruit. Those eyes gather so much light that a tarsier can pick a moth off a leaf on a night with no moon at all.

facts.text: The eyes are locked in their sockets — a tarsier cannot roll them. So it turns its head instead, about 180 degrees each way, enough to look back over its own spine.
Tarsiers are the only primates that eat no plants whatsoever. No fruit, no leaves, no seeds — only animals they catch: insects, spiders, lizards, small birds.
facts.more: Chimpanzees eat meat and so do baboons, but both eat plenty of fruit as well. Every mouthful a tarsier takes was alive a moment before. It snatches insects out of the air in mid-leap and pins them with both hands.

facts.text: It can cross 3 m (10 ft) of open air between two trunks — more than twenty times its own body length — and land feet-first, gripping bark instantly.
The name comes from its ankles. Two bones in each ankle, the tarsals, are stretched extra long, which turns a hand-sized animal into a spring-loaded launcher.
A tarsier can scream at a pitch you will never hear. Researchers recorded calls with a dominant frequency near 70 kHz — more than three times higher than human ears can catch.
facts.more: The same team tested tarsier hearing and found sensitivity reaching about 91 kHz, among the highest measured in any land mammal. To a person standing under the tree, the animal appears to open its mouth in complete silence.

facts.text: Its ears crumple and unfurl constantly, each one moving separately from the other, tracking a single insect through the dark by sound alone.
A newborn tarsier arrives finished: eyes already open, fur already grown, and able to climb within a day of being born.
facts.more: She sometimes parks the baby on a branch while she hunts, and carries it in her mouth the way a cat carries a kitten. Within a few weeks it is catching its own insects.

facts.text: By day it clings upright to a thin vertical stem deep inside a tangle of vegetation, sleeps there, and returns to the same few stems night after night.
The underside of its tail is ridged and callused, and the tarsier props on it like a third leg while clinging upright to a trunk.
Tarsiers do badly in captivity. A stressed one beats its head against the cage, and its skull is thin enough that this kills it. The honest answer to 'can I keep one' is no.
Wild tarsiers live only on certain islands of Southeast Asia — the Philippines, Borneo, Sulawesi and their neighbors — with different kinds on different islands.

wonder: Eyes too big to move, set in a head that turns almost the whole way round — one design answering another.

name: Vampire bat
blurb: A small bat of Mexico, Central and South America that lives on one food and one food only: the blood of sleeping animals.
size: About the size of a mouse — you could hold one in one hand

facts.text: Three kinds of bat in the world drink blood, and this is the one that goes for mammals — cattle, horses, pigs, tapirs. It eats nothing else. Ever.
Pits around its nose read heat. Held close to a sleeping animal, they show it exactly where a blood vessel runs nearest the skin — and that is where it bites.
facts.more: The nerve endings inside those pits are tuned to warmth rather than touch, so the bat effectively sees a heat map of the animal in front of it. Some snakes have a similar sense. Almost no other mammal does.

facts.text: It does not suck. Razor-edged front teeth open a shallow cut, and the blood runs up grooves along the sides of its tongue — lapped, the way a cat drinks milk.
facts.more: The cut is so shallow and the teeth so sharp that a sleeping cow usually never wakes. A meal takes about twenty minutes of quiet lapping, with the bat crouched on the ground or clinging to a leg.

facts.text: Its saliva carries an anticoagulant — a chemical that stops blood clotting — so the tiny wound keeps flowing the entire time it feeds.
facts.more: One of those proteins was named draculin, which is exactly the joke you think it is. Without it, a cut that small would seal itself within a minute or two and the bat would go to bed hungry.

facts.text: Doctors took an interest in that saliva. A clot-dissolving drug called desmoteplase, built from a vampire bat protein, has been tested on stroke patients, whose brains are damaged by clots.
A 40 g bat can drink over 20 g of blood — half its own weight. Blood is mostly water, so it starts urinating within two minutes of starting, shedding water as it drinks.
facts.more: Otherwise it would be far too heavy to take off. Afterwards its kidneys switch to the opposite job, producing thick, concentrated urine so the bat keeps every drop of water it can from the meal.

facts.text: Most bats are helpless on the ground. This one runs, in a bounding gait where the wings do the pushing instead of the legs.
facts.more: It matters because this bat feeds on the ground, creeping up on a sleeping animal's foot. Being able to bound sideways and spring into the air the instant a hoof moves is worth a great deal.

facts.text: A vampire bat that fails to feed for about two nights running will die. So a well-fed bat brings up part of its own meal and gives it, mouth to mouth, to a hungry roost-mate.
facts.more: Researchers have followed named individuals for years. Bats tend to share with the same partners over and over, and one that has donated is more likely to be fed when its own night goes badly. They keep track of each other.

facts.text: A pup drinks milk for months, then is fed blood mouth-to-mouth long before it hunts for itself. Some are still not fully weaned at nine months old.
Every bat's contact call is slightly different from every other, and roost-mates learn to tell one another apart by voice in a dark cave full of chatter.
It roosts in caves, hollow trees and old buildings in groups of dozens to hundreds, hanging in the dark and grooming one another for hours at a time.

wonder: Nose, tongue, teeth and kidneys — every one of them fitted for a diet of nothing but blood.

name: Flying fox
blurb: The largest bats on Earth: fruit-eating, dog-faced bats that hang by the thousand in noisy treetop camps and never use sonar at all.
size: Wings that open wider than you are tall — about 1.5 m (5 ft) in the biggest kinds

facts.text: The biggest flying foxes stretch about 1.5 m (5 ft) from wingtip to wingtip — wider than you are tall — while the body in the middle weighs around a kilogram (2 lb).
facts.more: Almost all that width is skin. A bat's wing is its hand: the four long fingers you can see running through the membrane are the same four fingers you have, drawn out thin and joined by living skin with blood moving through it.

facts.text: Flying foxes do not echolocate. No clicks, no sonar. They find their food with big forward-facing eyes and an excellent nose, the way you would find a bakery.
facts.more: Bats that hunt insects need sonar because a moth is small, fast and moving. A fruiting tree stays where it is and smells ripe from a long way off, so eyes and a nose do the job. 'Blind as a bat' was always nonsense.

facts.text: It squeezes the fruit against the roof of its mouth, swallows the juice, then spits out a dry pellet of skin and fiber. The ground under a feeding tree is scattered with them.
By day they hang in camps — hundreds or thousands of bats in one stand of trees, squabbling over the best branches, shuffling about, and audible from streets away.
It sleeps hanging by its feet, wrapped in its own wings like a folded umbrella. The toes lock shut under the bat's own weight, so hanging on costs almost no effort.
Durian flowers open after dark. Island flying foxes visit them for nectar, and when researchers watched closely, the trees the bats visited went on to set more fruit.
facts.more: Durian is the spiky, powerfully smelly fruit sold across Southeast Asia. A bat shoves its face into a blossom for nectar, comes away dusted in pollen, and carries that pollen to the next tree, sometimes kilometers away.

facts.text: A flying fox may cover up to 50 km (30 miles) in a night getting to a fruiting tree and home again — a commute longer than most people's.
facts.more: It can hold about 6 m per second, roughly 13 mph, for three hours at a stretch. Because they carry seeds and pollen that far, they replant forest as they go: a seed swallowed in one valley gets dropped in the next.

facts.text: A mother has a single pup a year. For its first weeks it flies with her, hooked to her chest by thumbs and feet, until it grows too heavy and stays behind in the camp.
That hook at the bend of each wing is a thumb, with a claw on it, left free of the membrane. Flying foxes carry a second claw on the index finger as well.
facts.more: Insect-hunting bats have the thumb claw only. A flying fox climbs with both, hauling itself hand over hand along a branch and holding food up to its mouth while it hangs by one foot.

facts.text: A camp is loud all day long. Flying foxes have a wide range of squabbling, warning and greeting calls, and a mother picks her own pup out of hundreds by call and by smell.
On dangerously hot days they fan themselves with their wings and lick their wrists and chests, so the wet fur cools them as it dries.

wonder: They eat the forest and replant it in the same night — feeding one thing feeds another.

name: Beaver
blurb: A thickset, buck-toothed rodent that cuts down trees with its teeth and rebuilds whole streams into ponds.
size: About the size of a Border Collie, with a flat leathery tail shaped like a paddle.

facts.text: A beaver's four front teeth never stop growing. It has to gnaw every day of its life, or they would grow right past its jaw.
facts.more: The front face of each incisor is hard, iron-rich enamel; the back is softer dentine. The soft side wears away faster, so every bite grinds the tooth back into a fresh chisel edge. A beaver's teeth sharpen themselves on the job.

facts.text: The longest beaver dam anyone has found runs 850 meters (2,790 feet) across a marsh in northern Alberta — longer than nine football fields end to end.
facts.more: It sits on the southern edge of Wood Buffalo National Park and was first spotted in satellite photographs. No single beaver built it. One family after another kept patching and extending the same wall until it ran clear across the wetland.

facts.text: Beavers build because of a sound. Play a recording of running water next to a beaver and it will pile mud and sticks on top of the loudspeaker.
facts.more: A Swedish biologist named Lars Wilsson tested exactly this. He offered beavers a real leak they could see, running almost silently, and a speaker trickling away on dry ground. They ignored the leak and dammed the speaker. The trigger is the noise.

facts.text: It reads the current. In slow water a beaver builds its dam straight across; in fast water it builds a curve, bowed against the push of the river.
A beaver has see-through third eyelids that slide across like swim goggles, and lips that shut behind its front teeth so it can chew a branch underwater without swallowing the pond.
Slap. A beaver whacks its tail flat on the water and the crack carries across the whole pond — the alarm that sends every beaver diving.
facts.more: Adults do not always fall for it. When a young beaver slaps at nothing much, the older ones often keep right on eating. A beaver can stay under for up to about fifteen minutes on one breath, so a false alarm costs it little.

facts.text: The front door is underwater. A beaver dives, swims up a tunnel and climbs out onto a dry shelf inside a dome of mud-plastered sticks.
facts.more: Towards winter the family smears wet mud over the outside. It freezes to the consistency of concrete and a wolf cannot dig through it. They leave the very top loose and airy on purpose — that patch is the chimney that lets everyone breathe.

facts.text: Beavers eat no fish at all. They eat bark — mostly the soft living layer just underneath it, called cambium — plus buds, roots and pond plants.
facts.more: Wood is close to impossible to digest. A beaver's gut carries microbes that break down cellulose for it, the same trick a cow uses on grass. Willow, aspen and poplar are the favourites, and branches get stashed underwater as a winter larder.

facts.text: Beavers mark their territory with mud pies. They scrape up a heap on the bank and dab it with castoreum, a goo from a gland under the tail that smells of vanilla.
facts.more: That is not a poetic description — castoreum genuinely smells sweet, and people have used it in perfume for a very long time. To another beaver the little mound is a signpost saying, plainly, this stretch of stream is taken.

facts.text: The beaver is the biggest rodent in North America, and the porcupine is second. A grown beaver weighs around 20 kg (44 lb) — about what a Border Collie weighs.
Kits are born furred, with their eyes already open, and can swim within days. They stay with their parents about two years, helping with dam repairs before setting off.
A beaver pond is a whole neighbourhood. Flooding the trees makes still water, and frogs, herons, dragonflies, moose and trout all move in behind the beaver.
facts.more: This is why beavers get called ecosystem engineers. One family cutting willows reshapes a valley — slowing floods, holding water through dry spells, and spreading a marsh where there used to be nothing but a narrow creek.

wonder: Goggles, sealing lips, a mud trowel of a tail, teeth that sharpen themselves — everything a dam-builder needs, given before the first dam was ever built.

name: Porcupine
blurb: A slow, shaggy, tree-climbing rodent with about thirty thousand sharp quills growing out through its fur.
size: About as heavy as a medium-sized dog, and it looks twice that size once the quills go up.

facts.text: A porcupine cannot throw its quills. Not one, not ever. It turns its back, hunches up and reverses at you — the quills release only when something touches them.
facts.more: The myth probably starts with the tail. A porcupine lashes it sideways, and if the tail strikes a rock, loose quills can fly off and travel a short way. It looks like a launch. It is really just a hard swing.

facts.text: The barbs that make a quill so hard to pull out are microscopic, and every one of them is crowded into the top four millimeters — a band about as wide as a grain of rice.
Engineers copied the quill. In the laboratory those barbs cut the push-in force roughly in half, and quadruple the force needed to drag the quill back out.
facts.more: Easy in, hard out is a strange combination — and exactly what surgeons want from a staple or a skin patch. A barbed quill even slides into tissue more easily than a hypodermic needle of the same thickness, so laboratories now build needles with quill-shaped barbs.

facts.text: It is the second-largest rodent in North America, after the beaver. Every one of those quills is really a hair: hollow, stiff, and up to three inches (75 mm) long.
A newborn porcupine is called a porcupette, and it arrives with its quills lying flat and soft as wet paper. They dry and stiffen within hours.
facts.more: It is born big — eyes open, whiskered, able to climb a tree within days. Mothers raise a single baby a year, which is very few for a rodent. Then again, almost nothing wants to eat an animal made of needles.

facts.text: Porcupines crave salt so badly they chew human things to get it: axe handles, canoe paddles, plywood, outhouse seats, road signs.
facts.more: A diet of bark and leaves is desperately low in sodium, so a porcupine hunts it wherever it can. Anything a sweaty hand has gripped for years tastes salty to them. Backpackers learn to hang their boots and tools well out of reach.

facts.text: In winter a porcupine eats bark and conifer needles — food so poor that it loses weight all season long and simply has to last until spring.
Quills are greasy, and the grease is antibiotic. It helps protect the porcupine from its own weapon.
facts.more: Porcupines fall out of trees more often than you would guess, and a falling porcupine lands squarely on its own points. The fatty acids coating each quill have antibiotic properties that help stop those self-inflicted wounds turning septic.

facts.text: Look at its hands. Long curved claws and rough, pebbly palms grip bark, and the stiff bristles under its tail dig in behind like a climber's spikes.
You smell a porcupine before you see one. It carries a strong sour odor — a warning broadcast on a second channel, in case you somehow missed the spikes.
One hunter has an answer to quills: the fisher, a big weasel that circles the porcupine's face and bites the bare nose until it can flip the animal over.
facts.more: The belly carries no quills at all, so the whole fight is about getting underneath. Fishers are agile climbers and will force a porcupine down out of a tree first, where it is far more vulnerable than it is up among the branches.

wonder: Thirty thousand needles, each one greased against infection — armor that also looks after the animal wearing it.

name: Striped skunk
blurb: A cat-sized black-and-white forager that can fire a foul-smelling chemical spray from two nozzles under its tail.
size: About the size of a housecat, with a bushy tail nearly as long as its body.

facts.text: The spray is a last resort. First comes the deimatic display: the skunk stamps its front feet, hisses, arches its back, fluffs up, and hoists that tail like a flag.
facts.more: Deimatic means startling — a bluff meant to make a bigger animal back off. Everything about a skunk is a warning it would much rather you took. The stripe is a signpost; the stamping is a countdown. Spraying costs the skunk something real.

facts.text: It aims. Two nozzles under the tail swivel and fire, and a skunk can hit your face with real accuracy from three meters (10 feet) away.
A skunk carries only about five or six shots — roughly a tablespoon in total. Once the glands run dry it can take up to ten days to refill them.
facts.more: Which is exactly why the warning dance matters so much. A skunk with empty glands still stamps and hisses and puffs up and hopes hard that the bluff works — because there is nothing at all behind it.

facts.text: The stink is made of thiols, which are sulfur compounds. Your nose picks them up at about eleven parts per billion — roughly one drop spread through twenty-five full bathtubs.
facts.more: Sulfur is the thread connecting rotten eggs, struck matches and skunks. Human noses are extraordinarily tuned to it, far more sensitive to thiols than to almost anything else we can smell, which is the skunk's whole business model.

facts.text: Skunk smell comes back. Part of the spray is a chemical with almost no odor until water touches it — then it turns into thiol and stinks all over again.
facts.more: That is why a washed dog smells fine when dry and dreadful in the rain. The culprits are thioacetates, hiding in the fur, waiting. Rinsing without neutralising them properly just sets up the next ambush.

facts.text: Tomato juice does not work. It only tires your nose out. The real fix is chemistry: hydrogen peroxide, baking soda and dish soap, mixed fresh in a bucket.
facts.more: A chemist named Paul Krebaum worked it out. The peroxide turns the thiols into compounds that have no smell at all, and the soap breaks up the oil so the peroxide can reach it. Mix it and use it at once — never seal it in a bottle.

facts.text: A skunk will dig a wasp nest out of the ground and eat the grubs, stings and all. Thick fur and loose skin shrug off the defense.
About housecat-sized, and the tail does a lot of the work — it fluffs out when the skunk is alarmed, making an animal of roughly 3 kg (7 lb) look far bigger.
A skunk can barely see you. Its eyes cannot make out objects much beyond three meters (10 feet), which is precisely why it stamps and postures at anything that comes close.
One hunter is not put off in the slightest. The great horned owl is the skunk's only regular predator — it flies in silence, and it hardly smells a thing.
facts.more: Owls have a famously weak sense of smell, so the skunk's entire chemical defense means very little to them. Naturalists sometimes find great horned owl nests that reek of skunk, and owls that carry the scent on their feathers for weeks.

facts.text: Skunks do not truly hibernate. They drop their body temperature and doze underground through the cold — often several females to a den — and wander out to feed on mild nights.
Kits are born blind, deaf and barely furred, weighing about as much as a slice of bread — and the stripe is already there, printed into the skin before the hair grows.

wonder: A creature that would far rather be believed than fight, wearing its warning sign in its own skin.

name: Nine-banded armadillo
blurb: A digging, insect-hunting mammal built inside a jointed shell of bony plates, like a small armoured car.
size: About as long as a housecat once you count the tail, and roughly as heavy as a bowling ball.

facts.text: Every litter is identical quadruplets. Nearly always four babies, all the same sex, all grown from a single fertilised egg that split into four.
facts.more: Almost nothing else on earth does this as a rule — only its close armadillo relatives. The four are as alike as identical twins, which is why medical researchers value them so highly: four subjects with exactly matching genes, raised in exactly the same burrow.

facts.text: It gulps air to swim. An armadillo swallows enough air to puff up its stomach and gut, turning a heavy armoured animal into something that floats.
facts.more: The other option is stranger still. If the creek is narrow, it simply walks in, sinks, and strolls across the bottom holding its breath for up to six minutes. Either way it reaches the far bank.

facts.text: Startle an armadillo and it launches straight up — about a meter (3 to 4 feet) into the air, all four feet off the ground at once.
facts.more: This works beautifully against a coyote and disastrously against a car. An armadillo low enough to pass safely underneath a vehicle instead jumps up into the bumper, which is why so many end up beside the road.

facts.text: It cannot roll into a ball. That is a different animal entirely — only the three-banded armadillos of South America can close themselves up into a sphere.
facts.more: A nine-banded armadillo's shell has no room to fold that far. Its plan is to run, or to wedge itself deep into a burrow and arch its back so hard against the roof that nothing can drag it out.

facts.text: Nearly blind, magnificent nose. An armadillo works a patch of ground by smell alone and can pin down a beetle grub twenty centimeters (8 inches) under the soil.
It eats mostly insects — beetles, termites, ants, grubs — plus millipedes, worms and the odd bird egg. Less than a tenth of its diet is anything other than animal.
Its teeth are just pegs. No canines, no enamel at all — a row of blunt little cylinders at the back and nothing whatsoever at the front to bite with.
The shell is real bone. Small plates called scutes grow inside the skin under a horny layer, with bands of soft flexible hide between them so the animal can still bend.
It digs constantly — burrows for sleeping, burrows for escaping, and a nest chamber stuffed with a huge ball of dry leaves raked in with its front claws.
facts.more: An armadillo sleeps up to sixteen hours a day underground and comes out around dusk. Abandoned burrows get taken over by snakes, rabbits, opossums and burrowing owls, so a single digger ends up housing a whole crowd.

facts.text: An armadillo runs cool. Its body sits around 34°C (93°F), a few degrees below yours, and it suffers badly in a hard frost.
facts.more: That low temperature is also why armadillos matter to medicine. The bacterium behind leprosy grows best below normal human body heat, and the armadillo is one of very few animals it can live inside — which is one good reason never to pick up a wild one.

facts.text: Nine-banded armadillos are the only armadillos found in the United States, and their range keeps pushing steadily further north.
Despite the name, the bands vary. Count the moveable bands around an armadillo's middle and you may find seven, or eleven — nine is simply the most common.

wonder: Armour, a nose that reads underground, and lungs that let it walk across a riverbed — one small animal issued three completely different toolkits.

name: Meerkat
blurb: A small, sharp-eyed African mongoose that lives in big underground families and posts a lookout while the others dig for food.
size: From nose to rump about the length of a school ruler, with a thin tail nearly as long again.

facts.text: Somebody is always watching. One meerkat climbs the highest thing around and scans the sky while the rest dig, then swaps out for the next volunteer.
facts.more: Sentries do not eat while on duty. They keep up a soft running murmur that researchers call the watchman's song — a steady all-clear that lets the diggers keep their heads down and their minds on the sand.

facts.text: Meerkat alarm calls carry two pieces of information at once: what the danger is, and how close it has already got.
facts.more: A call for an eagle sends everyone bolting for the nearest bolt-hole. A call for a snake or a jackal sends them bunching up instead. Urgency is coded separately, so a distant hawk gets a different call from one already diving.

facts.text: Adults teach. They hand pups live scorpions with the stings bitten off, and as the pups get better they pass over prey that is less and less disabled.
facts.more: This is one of the clearest cases of genuine teaching known outside our own species. The adults listen to the pups' begging calls to judge how old they are, then raise the difficulty. A live, fully armed scorpion is the final exam.

facts.text: A meerkat disarms a scorpion before it fights it — one fast bite that snips the stinger clean off the end of the tail.
facts.more: Pups who get the timing wrong really do get stung, and they squeal about it. Adults are quicker and far more precise, and they will strip the stinger off a scorpion before handing the rest to a pup that is still learning the job.

facts.text: A meerkat weighs about 730 grams (1.6 lb) — roughly a big bottle of water — and props itself upright on its hind legs, using its tail as the third leg of a tripod.
A membrane sweeps across each eye like a windscreen wiper while it digs, and the ears fold shut to keep the sand out. The front claws are long, curved hooks.
The burrow is a town: tunnels, sleeping chambers and around fifteen doorways, dug a meter and a half (5 feet) down and shared by up to thirty meerkats.
facts.more: The sand at the surface can get too hot to stand on, while the chambers far below stay cool and steady all day long. Each family owns several burrows across its territory and moves between them, so there is always somewhere to run.

facts.text: When the group goes foraging, some adults stay behind as babysitters — going a whole day without food to guard pups too young to leave the burrow.
Meerkats hardly drink at all. Almost everything they need comes out of what they eat, with roots and tsamma melons supplying water in the driest months.
facts.more: Insects make up most of the diet — beetle larvae, crickets, spiders, centipedes — plus lizards, eggs and the occasional small snake. A meerkat forages nearly all day and stores almost nothing away for later.

facts.text: The black patches around a meerkat's eyes cut the glare of the desert sun — the same job as the black stripes an American footballer paints under his.
Meerkats will mob a snake. The whole group bristles up, packs tight together and advances on it as one loud, spitting, much-larger-looking animal.
On a cold morning the family sits up and faces the sunrise. The belly fur is thin over dark skin, so they warm through like a row of small solar panels.

wonder: Lookouts, teachers, babysitters and a shared front door — a whole society packed into an animal lighter than a bottle of water.

name: Red kangaroo
blurb: The largest marsupial alive: a long-legged grazer that crosses the dry heart of Australia by hopping.
size: A big male stands about 5 ft (1.5 m) tall, chin height on a grown man, and can weigh as much as one

facts.text: Watch the back legs. In a short burst a red kangaroo hits about 35 mph (56 km/h), faster than any human sprinter who has ever lived.
facts.more: That is a sprint, not a cruise. Crossing open country it settles into a steady 15 mph (25 km/h) and holds that pace for miles, because at hopping speed the traveling costs it almost nothing extra.

facts.text: Its legs are springs. Enormous Achilles tendons stretch as it lands and snap back as it launches, so most of the energy for the next hop is recycled from the last one.
facts.more: Measure a hopping kangaroo's oxygen use and something odd shows up: as it speeds up, it does not breathe harder. The tendons are doing work the muscles would otherwise pay for. A galloping horse gets no such bargain.

facts.text: Slow it right down and the tail becomes a fifth leg. Shuffling along while it grazes, a kangaroo plants its tail and pushes as hard as the front and back legs combined.
facts.more: Researchers had kangaroos walk over plates that measure force. The tail was not merely propping the animal up. It was doing about as much pushing work as one of your legs does when you walk.

facts.text: A newborn red kangaroo is the size of a jellybean, about an inch (2.5 cm) long, pink, blind and deaf. And it makes the climb to the pouch entirely on its own.
facts.more: Roughly 33 days after mating, the joey is born with its hind legs barely formed but its front arms already strong and clawed. It hauls itself up through its mother's fur, finds a teat, and stays attached for months.

facts.text: A mother kangaroo can press pause. When the rain fails, a tiny embryo simply stops developing and waits, sometimes for months, until the country is good enough to raise it.
facts.more: The pause is called embryonic diapause. It means a female can have a joey at heel, another in the pouch, and a third on hold, all at once, ready to restart the moment the grass comes back.

facts.text: Grass wears teeth down to stumps. So a kangaroo's worn front molars drop out and the teeth behind slide forward to replace them, the whole row creeping along like a conveyor belt.
facts.more: Each side of the jaw gets four grinding molars, arriving one at a time across a kangaroo's life. When the last one is worn flat there is no replacement behind it, and a very old kangaroo can no longer chew tough grass.

facts.text: On a scorching day a kangaroo licks its own forearms. The skin there is thin with blood vessels close beneath, so evaporating spit chills the blood on its way back inside.
facts.more: It is the same trick as a wet cloth on the back of your neck, done deliberately and over and over. Kangaroos also lie up in shade through the worst hours and do most of their feeding at dusk and dawn.

facts.text: Red kangaroos live where the creeks stay dry for months at a stretch. They can go a long time without drinking, pulling most of the water they need straight out of green plants.
Males box, but the boxing is not the weapon. A kangaroo leans back on its tail like a tripod and drives both hind feet forward, claws first, with its whole weight behind them.
Its ears swivel separately, each one turning toward a different sound, while the head stays down in the grass and carries on eating.
Danger gets announced with a foot. A kangaroo thumps a hind leg hard against the ground, and every head in the mob comes up at once.
A kangaroo cannot hop backwards. That heavy tail and those long feet only work in one direction, so to retreat it has to turn its whole body around first.

wonder: Springs for legs, a fifth leg for a tail, and a pause button for the hard years. Every part of it fits the country it was put in.

name: Koala
blurb: A thick-furred, tree-living marsupial from eastern Australia that eats almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves. Not a bear.
size: About the size of a very well-fed house cat, with a much larger head and no tail to speak of

facts.text: Eucalyptus leaves are loaded with oils and toxins that would make most animals sick. A koala's liver takes those toxins apart and flushes them out in its urine.
facts.more: Almost nothing else competes for this food, which is exactly why it works. The price is that the leaves are tough, watery and poor in energy, so a koala's entire day is arranged around not wasting any.

facts.text: Inside the koala is a fermenting tank. The caecum, a blind pouch off the gut, runs about 6.5 ft (2 m), which is longer than the koala it lives inside.
facts.more: Millions of microbes live in there, slowly breaking down leaf fiber the koala's own body cannot touch. A meal can sit fermenting for days. That long, patient gut is how something cat-sized survives on something so poor.

facts.text: Up to 20 hours a day dozing or sitting perfectly still. That is not laziness. Eucalyptus gives back so little energy that a koala genuinely cannot afford to spend much.
A koala joey's first solid food is a soft green paste called pap, produced in its mother's gut and eaten straight from her.
facts.more: Pap is not ordinary droppings. It comes from the caecum and is crowded with living microbes. Without that mouthful the joey could never digest eucalyptus at all, so its mother is handing over her gut bacteria along with the meal.

facts.text: Shut your eyes near a bellowing male koala and you would guess at something enormous. He has an extra pair of vocal folds sitting where the nose and throat meet.
facts.more: Most mammals make sound with folds inside the voice box. The male koala has a second, far larger pair outside it, about three times longer and hundreds of times heavier, which is how an animal you could lift produces a bass roar.

facts.text: Koalas have fingerprints. Real ones, with loops and arches and whorls, so close to human prints that under a microscope even experts can confuse the two.
Look at the hands. Each front paw has two thumbs instead of one, so the grip closes on a branch from both sides at once, like a pair of pliers.
facts.more: The back feet are stranger still. The second and third toes are joined inside a single sheath with two claws poking out the end, and the koala uses that double claw as a comb for its fur.

facts.text: When rain runs down a tree trunk, koalas lick it off the bark. Researchers watching wild koalas recorded them drinking that way for many minutes at a stretch.
On a blazing day a koala presses itself flat against a tree trunk. Thermal cameras show the trunk can sit several degrees cooler than the air around it.
facts.more: Measurements have found trunks up to about 9 degrees F (5 degrees C) below air temperature. A koala hugging one is doing what you do lying on cool tiles, and it can be the difference between surviving a heatwave and not.

facts.text: The joey is born blind, hairless and jellybean-sized, into a pouch that opens downward. A ring of muscle around the opening keeps it from dropping out.
That big leathery nose does the choosing. A koala sniffs a leaf before it bites, and turns down far more than it accepts, even in a tree it feeds in daily.
A koala from the cool southern forests can be roughly twice the weight of a northern one, about 26 lb (12 kg) against 14 lb (6.5 kg), with shaggier, greyer fur.

wonder: A whole animal built around one poisonous tree, right down to the gut bacteria a mother hands to her child.

name: Wombat
blurb: A barrel-shaped Australian marsupial that digs long tunnel systems and comes out at night to graze.
size: Knee-high and shaped like a barrel, about the weight of a large and extremely solid dog

facts.text: Wombat droppings come out as cubes. Eighty to a hundred of them a night, and the wombat balances them on rocks and logs where other wombats will find them.
facts.more: Scientists who studied wombat intestines found the last stretch is not evenly stretchy. Stiff patches and soft patches squeeze the drying pellets into flat sides. A cube stays put on a rock. A ball rolls off. That is the whole point.

facts.text: Its backside is armor: a thick pad of cartilage under tough hide and coarse fur, with barely any bone in it. A wombat reverses into its tunnel and blocks the doorway.
One burrow can run 65 ft (20 m) underground, with side tunnels and sleeping chambers off the main shaft. About two-thirds of a wombat's life happens down there.
facts.more: Below ground the temperature barely moves, whatever the weather is doing above. That is how a thick-furred animal survives blazing summers. The wombat is carrying its own cool room around with it, dug by hand.

facts.text: Grass, and a great deal of chewing. Digesting a single meal takes a wombat 8 to 14 days, one of the slowest digestions known in any mammal.
facts.more: Slow is the point. The longer food sits, the more water and nourishment gets wrung out of it, which matters when your diet is dry native grass and the nearest creek is nowhere. Wombat droppings come out remarkably dry.

facts.text: Every one of a wombat's teeth keeps growing for its whole life, because grinding gritty grass and roots would otherwise wear them away to nothing.
The pouch faces backwards. A digging wombat hurls dirt out behind itself, so a forward-facing pouch would pack solid with soil and bury the joey inside it.
It looks like a barrel on legs, but a wombat can hit 25 mph (40 km/h) in a short dash, quick enough to beat most people back to the burrow.
Wombat tunnels get used by animals that never dug them. Cameras set at burrow entrances have filmed small mammals, lizards and birds going in and coming back out.
facts.more: The wombat does not invite them and mostly does not appear to mind. One animal's hard work ends up sheltering a whole neighbourhood, which is why researchers call the wombat an engineer of its landscape.

facts.text: It is the largest burrowing plant-eater on earth. Around 57 lb (26 kg) of muscle, claw and bone, built low to the ground for shoving through soil.
Weak eyes, superb nose and ears. A wombat works the dark by smell, including reading which wombat left which cube on which rock.
Cornered underground, a wombat does not turn and fight. It braces its legs and jams that armoured rump up into the tunnel roof, and the doorway simply closes.
The hot part of the day is spent asleep underground. A wombat surfaces around dusk and grazes for hours, sometimes traveling well beyond its own burrow.

wonder: Shovels at the front, armor at the back, and a gut that turns dry grass into a signpost.

name: Tasmanian devil
blurb: The largest meat-eating marsupial alive: a stocky, black, night-roaming scavenger found wild only in Tasmania.
size: About the size of a small, very stout dog, standing only around a foot (30 cm) at the shoulder

facts.text: For its size, no living mammal bites harder. Pound for pound a devil's jaws out-bite a lion's, and it uses them to crunch straight through leg bone.
facts.more: Scientists compare bites using a bite force quotient, which measures bite strength against body size. The devil scores around 181, while a lion comes in near 112. A devil's head is very nearly all jaw muscle.

facts.text: Nothing gets left behind. A devil eats the skin, the fur, the organs and the bones, and a dead wallaby can vanish overnight with barely a stain on the grass.
Given half an hour alone with a carcass, a devil can put away 40% of its own body weight. For you that would be roughly 25 school lunches in one sitting.
facts.more: Biologists call it gorge feeding. Devils compete hard for whatever has died, so the first one there eats as much and as fast as it possibly can before the next one shoves in. A well-fed devil walks away visibly swollen.

facts.text: A mother devil gives birth to 20 or 30 young at once. She has four teats. Only the first four to arrive will ever feed.
facts.more: Each newborn is about the size of a grain of rice. They must crawl through her fur into a backward-facing pouch and latch on. Those four stay attached for around 100 days, then wait in a den while she hunts.

facts.text: The name came from the noise. Devils have at least eleven distinct calls, including snorts, growls, coughs and a screech that carries a long way through dark bush.
facts.more: Most of the racket is bluff. A crowd of devils around a carcass screams, gapes and shoves, and the noise largely settles who eats first without anybody getting badly hurt. Loud is cheaper than injured.

facts.text: When a devil is excited or upset, its ears turn red. Blood floods the thin bare skin there, and its mood becomes visible from across a clearing.
Satellite collars show devils covering about 5 miles (8.6 km) on an average night, criss-crossing their patch looking for anything that has died.
A devil keeps its savings in its tail. A thick, fat tail means an animal in good condition; a thin, ropy one is the first sign something is wrong.
It works the dark by nose and whisker. Long whiskers sweep out to about shoulder width, feeling the edges of things the devil cannot see.
Days are spent asleep in a den: a hollow log, a cave, a thicket of dense grass, and quite often a burrow that some wombat dug and abandoned.
This is the biggest meat-eating marsupial on earth, and a male still averages only about 18 lb (8 kg), no heavier than a very large house cat.
Devils rarely chase down healthy adult prey. They find what has already died, which keeps the bush clean and stops flies and disease building up around carcasses.
facts.more: Farmers in Tasmania have long noticed that a paddock with devils working it has far fewer rotting carcasses in it. The animal with the worst reputation on the island is mostly doing the tidying up.

wonder: Nothing goes to waste in a forest that has a devil in it. The clean-up crew arrives with its own bone-cracking jaws.

name: African elephant
blurb: The largest animal that walks on land, and the only one with a trunk that works as both a nose and a hand.
size: A big bull stands taller than a basketball hoop and weighs about as much as four family cars

facts.text: Nothing walking on land is bigger. A large bull stands over 10 ft (3.2 m) at the shoulder and can reach 6 tonnes (13,000 lb), which is roughly four cars.
There is no bone anywhere in the trunk. Tens of thousands of separate muscle bundles run through it, pulling against each other. Your entire body contains about 600 muscles.
facts.more: That is what makes it a crane and a pair of tweezers at once. The same trunk lifts a fallen branch and then picks up a single blade of grass. At the tip, an African elephant has two finger-like points that pinch together.

facts.text: An elephant does not drink through its trunk. It sucks water up, holds around 2 gallons (8 liters) in there, then curls the trunk into its mouth and squirts.
An adult puts away up to 330 lb (150 kg) of grass, bark and branches every day, and spends most of its waking hours doing it.
facts.more: It drinks 50 to 60 gallons (180 to 230 liters) a day as well. Feeding that body is close to a full-time job, which is why herds are always walking, and why the routes to water get remembered so carefully.

facts.text: Elephant molars are the size of bricks, and an elephant gets six sets in a lifetime. As one wears down it is pushed forward and out, and a fresh one moves up behind.
facts.more: Only about four grinding teeth are in use at any moment. When the sixth and final set is worn flat, no replacement is coming, and very old elephants shift to soft marsh grasses that need less grinding.

facts.text: Elephants talk in rumbles pitched too low for human ears, and those calls carry for kilometers across open country while you stand there hearing nothing at all.
facts.more: The sound travels through the ground as well as the air. In playback experiments, elephants given a rumble through the soil alone, with nothing audible above it, froze and turned toward it. They pick the vibration up through their feet and trunk.

facts.text: Smell is its main sense, not sight. The African elephant carries roughly 2,000 working genes for detecting odor, about five times as many as you have.
An African elephant has the largest ears of any animal alive, and they are radiators. Big blood vessels run just beneath that thin skin, and flapping them cools the blood on its way back inside.
An elephant barely sweats. It has no sweat glands anywhere on its body except between its toes, so its skin is covered instead in millions of hair-thin channels that hold water.
facts.more: That is why a mud bath is not only play. The cracked surface traps water and mud instead of shedding it, so one wallow keeps evaporating and cooling for hours, and the coating shields the skin from sun and biting insects.

facts.text: Pregnancy lasts 22 months, longer than any other mammal. The calf is born at around 250 lb (115 kg), heavier than a grown man, and is up on its feet within hours.
The herd follows its oldest female. Families led by older matriarchs proved better at telling a stranger's call from a friend's, so the group's memory really does live in her.
facts.more: During one severe drought, herds whose matriarchs had lived through an earlier dry spell led their families out to distant water, and lost fewer calves than herds without that experience at the front.

facts.text: An elephant cannot jump. No adult has ever been recorded with all four feet off the ground at once. The leg bones stack straight down like pillars, with no spring in them.

wonder: A nose with no bone in it that can shove over a tree, then lift a single seed. Strength and gentleness built into the same tool.

name: Moose
blurb: The biggest deer on Earth — a lanky, hump-shouldered giant that wades through northern ponds pulling up water plants.
size: A big bull stands about 6 feet (1.8 m) at the shoulder — eye to eye with a tall man, before you count the head and antlers

facts.text: A big Alaskan bull can pass 1,500 pounds (680 kg) and stand six feet (1.8 m) at the shoulder. His back is higher than the roof of a car.
facts.more: Moose are the largest deer on Earth. Those long legs are working legs — for wading through chest-deep snow in winter and pond mud in summer. A moose can step over a fallen log that a horse would have to walk around.

facts.text: Every summer a bull grows a whole set of antlers, then drops them in winter. At peak growth they can add close to an inch (2.5 cm) of bone a day.
facts.more: That makes antler one of the fastest-growing tissues in the animal world — a full rack in three to five months. While it grows it is wrapped in furry skin called velvet, packed with blood vessels feeding the bone underneath. Once the antler hardens, the velvet dries and the bull rubs it off against trees.

facts.text: The widest moose antlers ever recorded spanned close to 7 feet (2.1 m) tip to tip — wider than a standard doorway is tall.
facts.more: Big antlers are partly a signal. A cow can read a bull's condition off his headgear at a glance, and two rival bulls often size each other up and walk away without ever fighting.

facts.text: A moose eats 40 to 60 pounds (18-27 kg) of leaves, twigs and pond weed a day — a wheelbarrow of salad, gathered one mouthful at a time.
facts.more: Moose are browsers, not grazers: they strip leaves and twig-tips from shrubs rather than crop grass. In winter they live largely on frozen willow and birch twigs, and can spend eight hours of the day feeding.

facts.text: That vast nose is a valve. A moose can seal its nostrils shut, put its whole head under, and feed off the pond floor for half a minute at a time.
facts.more: Fatty pads and muscle inside the muzzle pinch the nostrils closed, so a feeding moose does not inhale pond water. Moose have been recorded diving more than 18 feet (5.5 m) — deeper than the deep end of a swimming pool — and they are the only deer that regularly feeds completely submerged.

facts.text: Moose hair is hollow. Every strand is a tiny air-filled tube, which traps warmth in brutal cold and doubles as a life jacket when the moose swims.
facts.more: Under the long guard hairs lies a dense wooly layer. Together they keep a moose comfortable in weather that would kill most animals — and buoyant enough to float while it feeds out in a lake.

facts.text: A moose runs 35 mph (56 km/h) through timber so thick you could not walk it, and swims steadily for hours without ever touching the bottom.
facts.more: Moose have been recorded crossing lakes ten miles (16 km) wide, moving at around 6 mph (10 km/h). Water is not an obstacle to a moose — it is a highway, an escape route from wolves, and a salad bar all at once.

facts.text: A newborn calf weighs under 30 pounds (13 kg) — less than a big dog. By its first winter that same calf can top 300 pounds (140 kg).
facts.more: Moose milk is far richer than cow's milk, and a calf puts on weight faster than almost any land mammal its size. It stays glued to its mother for a year — then she drives it off, just before the next calf arrives.

facts.text: Forget the antlers. A moose's real weapon is its front feet. It rears up and strikes downward, and it can kick in any direction, including sideways.
facts.more: Wildlife officers in Alaska report that moose injure more people there each year than bears do — almost always because somebody crowded a cow with a calf. Flattened ears and raised neck hair mean back away now.

facts.text: A moose's eyesight is poor — a person standing still can look like a stump. But each ear swivels on its own, and its nose is superb. It smells you first.
The flap of skin swinging under a moose's throat is called the bell. Its shape changes as a bull ages, and in fall it carries his scent through the forest.
facts.more: Nobody has fully settled what the bell is for. During the fall rut a bull digs a shallow wallow, soaks it in his own scent, and the dangling bell spreads that smell everywhere he walks.

facts.text: Moose are built for cold and suffer in heat. On a warm day one will stand chest-deep in a pond for hours — which is exactly where photographers find them.

wonder: God gave the moose a nose that seals like a valve, so a land animal could graze the bottom of a lake.

name: Pronghorn
blurb: A tan-and-white speedster of the North American plains that looks like an antelope, isn't one, and is the finest long-distance runner on land.
size: Shoulder about waist-high on an adult — roughly 3 feet (90 cm) — and about as heavy as a large dog

facts.text: Nothing in North America is faster. A pronghorn hits about 55 mph (88 km/h) — and unlike a cheetah, it does not then have to stop and pant.
facts.more: A cheetah's sprint is over in well under a minute. The pronghorn's run has no stop button — it holds hard speed mile after mile, which is a completely different kind of fast.

facts.text: The endurance is the astonishing part. A pronghorn can hold 35 mph (56 km/h) for four miles (6.4 km) — a racehorse would be finished long before.
facts.more: The engine explains it. A pronghorn's heart, windpipe and lungs are all outsized for its body, and it takes in oxygen several times faster than an animal that size normally could.

facts.text: Pronghorn horns do something no other animal's do: the outer sheath slides off every year and grows back. And they are pronged — a forward hook plus the main spike.
facts.more: Underneath sits a permanent bony core. The sheath is keratin, the same material as your fingernails, formed from fused hair. Males drop theirs in late fall and have a complete new set by the end of the following summer.

facts.text: It is not an antelope. True antelope live in Africa and Asia. The pronghorn sits in a family entirely its own — there is nothing else quite like it anywhere on Earth.
Its eyes are huge for its skull, set high and wide on the head. A pronghorn watches roughly 320 degrees around itself — nearly a full circle — without turning its head.
facts.more: Out on open prairie there is nothing to hide behind, so spotting a problem two ridges away is the entire survival plan. A pronghorn can pick out movement a very long way off and simply leave early.

facts.text: One Wyoming herd walks over 150 miles (240 km) each way, twice a year, squeezing through a high mountain pass to reach its winter range.
facts.more: It is called the Path of the Pronghorn. At one point the route narrows to a tight bottleneck, and Wyoming built wildlife overpasses across a busy highway there so the herd could keep using the road it has always used.

facts.text: A pronghorn can outrun almost anything, but a wire fence stops it cold. It does not jump — it drops flat and scrapes underneath, so a low bottom wire is a wall.
facts.more: Ranchers and biologists now build wildlife-friendly fence with the bottom wire raised and smooth, about 18 inches (45 cm) off the ground. Pronghorn slide straight under it; cattle still stay where they are put.

facts.text: When a pronghorn spots danger it flares the white hairs on its rump into a bright disc. Other pronghorn far across the prairie see the flash — and a scent goes with it.
facts.more: Muscles under the skin lift the long white hairs so the patch seems to double in size. A gland in that same patch releases a strong smell at the same moment, so one alarm travels by eye and by nose together.

facts.text: A fawn is standing within half an hour and can outrun a human within its first week. Twins are normal, and the mother hides them far apart from each other.
facts.more: Two fawns stashed a hundred meters apart means one coyote finding one does not cost her both. She returns only to nurse, then leaves again — a still, nearly scentless fawn is safer than a guarded one.

facts.text: Pronghorn eat sagebrush — bitter, oily stuff most grazers refuse — and through the dry months pull much of the water they need straight out of the plants they are chewing.
No burrow, no cliff, no cover. A pronghorn's whole defense is noticing trouble early and leaving before it arrives.

wonder: Eyes, lungs, heart and legs all sized to one purpose — every part of a pronghorn agrees with every other part.

name: Mountain goat
blurb: A shaggy white climber of North America's highest cliffs, at home on ledges barely wider than a book.
size: A big billy weighs up to 300 pounds (140 kg) — about as much as two grown men — with a shoulder hump of solid muscle

facts.text: Look at those feet. Each hoof splits into two toes that spread wide for balance, with a rubbery pad in the middle that grips bare rock like a climbing shoe.
facts.more: The outer rim is hard, for biting onto tiny edges; the inner pad is soft and tacky, for friction on smooth stone. Behind each hoof, sharp dewclaws dig in as brakes on the way back down.

facts.text: Mountain goats work slopes steeper than 60 degrees — far steeper than any staircase you have climbed — and can leap nearly 12 feet (3.6 m) from one ledge to the next.
It isn't actually a goat. Zoologists file it with the chamois and the serows, in a group called goat-antelopes. Your farmyard goat is a different animal entirely.
The coat is really two coats: dense wool underneath for warmth, long hollow guard hairs on top to shed wind and snow. It can sit out a blizzard on an open ridge.
