facts.more: In spring the whole thing comes off in ragged sheets and the goat looks like it lost a fight with a duvet. Tufts of shed wool end up caught on rocks and shrubs all over the summer range.

facts.text: In winter almost nothing grows up there. Goats paw snow off ledges for frozen grass, then eat lichen, moss and woody twigs that most animals would walk straight past.
Mountain goats crave salt. Their plant diet gives them almost no sodium, so they will travel miles and hang off a near-vertical mineral lick to lick the rock itself.
In some national parks goats shadow hikers — not for sandwiches, but for the salt in human sweat and urine. Rangers ask visitors to pee well off the trail.
facts.more: A goat that learns people mean salt stops being wary of people, and a wild animal with dagger horns standing next to a hiker is a problem for both of them. Some parks have moved habituated goats elsewhere.

facts.text: Mountain goats do not head-butt like rams. Those black horns are barely a hand long but needle-sharp, and a fight means stabbing sideways at the other goat's flank.
facts.more: They carry armor for exactly that: the skin over a mountain goat's rump is unusually thick and tough, protecting the part most likely to get jabbed. Serious fights are rare, and threat displays usually settle the argument.

facts.text: A kid is born on a ledge, stands within minutes, and is following its mother along cliff paths within days. There is no flat ground up there to practice on.
The bosses are the females. Nannies outrank the much larger billies, push them off the best feeding ledges, and a big billy will back down rather than argue.
Mountain goats live above the treeline as high as 13,000 feet (4,000 m), in wind that can hit 99 mph (160 km/h) and cold near minus 50°F (minus 46°C).
facts.more: That is hurricane wind and freezer cold, on bare rock, all winter, with no shelter to speak of. A goat simply turns its back to the weather, tucks in behind a boulder if there is one, and waits it out.

facts.text: The power is all up front. A humped shoulder and a heavy neck let a goat haul itself upward, the way you would pull yourself over the top of a high wall.

wonder: Feet, coat, shoulders and nerve, all fitted to one address — the last few hundred feet of the mountain, where nothing else can follow.

name: Chimpanzee
blurb: A powerful, noisy, tool-making ape of African forests and woodlands, living in big communities where everybody knows everybody.
size: Standing, roughly 4 to 5 feet (1.2-1.5 m) — shorter than most adults — but built far heavier through the chest, shoulders and arms

facts.text: Pound for pound, chimpanzee muscle pulls about a third harder than yours. The difference isn't magic — it comes down to fiber type.
facts.more: Chimp muscle is roughly two-thirds fast-twitch fiber, the explosive kind that pulls hard and briefly. Human muscle leans toward slow-twitch fiber, the kind that keeps going for hours. Individual fibers are much alike; it is the mix that differs.

facts.text: Chimps carry tool kits. In the Congo a chimp uses a stout stick to punch a hole into a termite nest, then a thinner stem with the tip chewed into a brush to fish termites out.
facts.more: The frayed brush tip catches far more termites than a plain stick does. Different communities make different designs and pass them to their young, which is why researchers talk about chimpanzee cultures — local ways of doing things.

facts.text: In West Africa chimps crack rock-hard nuts with a stone hammer on a stone anvil. It takes a young chimp years of clumsy practice before it actually works.
facts.more: Mothers leave nuts and stones set up correctly for their children, and sometimes crack one slowly right in front of them. The youngster copies, misses, copies again — and meanwhile eats the kernels its mother hands over.

facts.text: At Fongoli in Senegal, chimps snap off a branch, strip it, chew the end to a point, and jab it into hollow trunks to hunt sleeping bushbabies. Mostly females and youngsters do it.
facts.more: It is the first record of a non-human primate making a weapon to hunt with. It does not often succeed — in the first study, roughly one jab in twenty-two produced a catch — but the tool is deliberately shaped every single time.

facts.text: A chimp drums on the flat buttress roots of a big tree. The boom travels over a kilometer (0.6 miles) through forest, and each drummer has his own rhythm.
facts.more: Researchers in Uganda's Budongo Forest learned to name the drummer from sound alone — one male hammered out fast, evenly spaced beats, another a stuttering pattern. Chimps drum most while traveling, a way of saying where they are.

facts.text: A sick chimp will peel a shoot of a bitter plant it normally refuses and chew the pith. Within about a day, the parasite eggs in its droppings drop off sharply.
facts.more: The plant is Vernonia, and it is genuinely foul — healthy chimps will not touch it. It carries compounds that suppress a gut worm which can kill a chimp. One study found around 88% fewer worm eggs a day after a chimp chewed the pith.

facts.text: Chimps hunt monkeys as a team, and different chimps take different jobs — one driving the prey along a branch while others move ahead to cut off the escape routes.
facts.more: Afterwards the meat is shared, but not equally. Who gets a piece depends on who helped in the hunt, who is high-ranking, and who is a friend. Begging with an outstretched open hand often works.

facts.text: A chimp baby rides its mother for years — belly-first at the start, then piggyback — and still nurses well past its third birthday. Some stay near her into their teens.
Every evening, in about five minutes, a chimp bends branches into a springy bowl high in a tree and sleeps in it. The next night, it usually builds a fresh one.
A chimp community can hold 15 to 150 members, but they are almost never all in one place. They split into small parties and rejoin — scientists call this fission-fusion.
Parties of males patrol the edge of their territory in single file, silent, hair standing on end, stopping to listen. Chimpanzee borders are taken extremely seriously.
In a Japanese lab, young chimps beat adult humans at a memory test: numbers flash on a screen for a fraction of a second, then vanish, and the chimp taps them back in order.
facts.more: The numbers appeared for less than a second before being hidden behind blank white squares. The young chimps were both faster and more accurate than the university students tested against them.

wonder: Hands made for gripping branches turn out to fish, hammer, drum and heal — one design doing a dozen different jobs.

name: Orangutan
blurb: A huge, ginger, unhurried ape that spends almost its entire life up in the trees of Borneo and Sumatra.
size: A big male weighs about as much as a grown man — up to 200 pounds (90 kg) — with an arm span near 6 feet 7 inches (2 m)

facts.text: Stretch your arms out wide. Now imagine them longer than you are tall. A male's arm span reaches about 6 feet 7 inches (2 m) while he stands only around 4.5 feet (1.4 m).
facts.more: The shoulder joint swings almost anywhere, the fingers hook like grappling irons, and the feet grip as well as the hands do. An orangutan effectively has four hands, with hips loose enough to point its legs in any direction.

facts.text: Orangutans rarely jump. To cross a gap they climb a slender tree and rock it back and forth until it leans far enough to hand them across to the next one.
facts.more: Swaying costs far less energy than leaping, and it is far safer for an animal this heavy. A fall from the canopy would be serious, so an orangutan keeps at least two limbs holding on almost all of the time.

facts.text: An orangutan knows hundreds of tree species and roughly when each one will fruit. It has to — this forest fruits unpredictably, and a wrong guess means a wasted climb.
facts.more: Favourites include figs and durian, a spiky fruit that smells like old socks and tastes like custard. In lean months orangutans fall back on bark, leaves and termites, and can lose noticeable weight.

facts.text: No great ape waits longer between babies. A wild orangutan mother gives birth once every six to nine years, and the same infant is still with her for most of that time.
facts.more: The pay-off is that almost every infant survives. She is teaching one apprentice at a time, and the lessons genuinely take that long — which tree is fruiting, how to open it, how to build a bed that holds.

facts.text: Every evening an orangutan builds a bed: a frame of thick bent branches, a mattress of leafy twigs woven on top, sometimes a pillow and a roof against the rain.
facts.more: Researchers who tested the nests found orangutans pick stiffer branches for the load-bearing frame and thinner, springier ones for the mattress — the same idea as a bed base and a duvet. Then they build a brand new one the next night.

facts.text: A male called Rakus, cut in a fight, chewed the leaves of a vine and pressed the pulp onto the wound on his face, over and over. Within five days the wound had closed.
facts.more: The vine, Fibraurea tinctoria, is used as medicine by people living nearby, and lab tests find it both antibacterial and pain-relieving. This was the first careful record of a wild animal treating a wound with a plant that actually works.

facts.text: When an orangutan is uneasy it makes a sharp kiss-squeak. Hold a handful of leaves in front of the mouth and the same squeak drops in pitch — making the caller sound far bigger than it is.
facts.more: Pitch normally gives away body size: the bigger the animal, the deeper the call. Leaves held to the lips drag the squeak lower, so a smallish orangutan can sound like a heavyweight. Only some populations have the trick.

facts.text: A big male throws his head back and roars for minutes at a stretch. The long call carries more than half a mile (about 1 km) through dense forest.
facts.more: The throat sac under his chin works as a resonator, the way the hollow body of a guitar amplifies a string. Females walk toward the call; rival males quietly walk the other way.

facts.text: Only some adult males grow the huge cheek flanges. Others keep a slim face for years — and can start growing flanges later if the dominant male in the area disappears.
facts.more: The flanges are pads of fibrous and fatty tissue, and they develop under the push of testosterone. Two adult males of exactly the same age can look like two entirely different animals.

facts.text: In one Sumatran swamp, orangutans strip a twig and poke it into a Neesia fruit to flick the seeds out, because the fruit is stuffed with stinging fibreglass-like hairs.
facts.more: Orangutans on the other side of the river, with the same fruit and the same twigs available, do not do this. The trick is a local invention, passed along by watching somebody else — not something every orangutan is born knowing.

facts.text: Orangutans are the only great apes in Asia, and they live wild in exactly two places: the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. The name means 'person of the forest' in Malay.
Most big apes live in groups. An adult orangutan usually travels alone — one fruiting tree rarely feeds a crowd, so the forest keeps them spread thin across the canopy.
facts.more: Mothers with young are the exception, and orangutans will feed peacefully together in a heavily loaded tree. Daughters often settle near their mothers, so the ape in the next valley is quite often a relative.

wonder: Four gripping hands, a bed built fresh each night, and a mother who teaches one child at a time — a life fitted exactly to the canopy.

name: Arctic fox
blurb: A small, deep-furred fox that lives farther north than almost any other land animal and stays out hunting all winter.
size: About the size of a house cat, with a tail as thick as your arm

facts.text: Turn one paw over and even the soles are furred, pads and all. Its scientific name, Vulpes lagopus, means "hare-foot" — no other wild dog has this.
facts.more: That fur does two jobs: it grips ice like a rubber sole, and it lifts the pads off frozen ground. Blood vessels in the legs run a countercurrent exchange, warming blood on the way back up, so the feet sit just above freezing without draining heat from the body.

facts.text: An Arctic fox can curl up on open snow at -50 C (-58 F) and go to sleep. No burrow, no shelter. Its winter coat is among the best insulation ever measured on a mammal.
facts.more: The coat roughly doubles in thickness for winter, and the fox wraps that bushy tail over its face like a scarf. Everything else is tucked in too — short muzzle, short legs, small round ears. Less body sticking out means less heat leaking away.

facts.text: Twice a year it changes clothes. White from nose to tail in winter, then a patchy brown-gray for summer. No other wild dog swaps color with the seasons.
facts.more: The moult is triggered by changing daylight, not by snowfall. So in a late spring a fox can end up brilliant white on bare brown tundra for a few awkward weeks, visible to every eagle for miles. Coastal "blue" foxes skip white altogether and stay smoky gray all year.

facts.text: It hears a lemming moving under the snow, lines itself up, and dives headfirst — punching through the crust with its front feet to pin prey it never saw.
facts.more: Snow can bury a lemming completely, so the hunt is done entirely by ear. The fox tilts its head to pinpoint the rustle, springs almost straight up, and comes down nose-first, driving both forefeet through the crust to trap whatever is moving below.

facts.text: Arctic foxes raise some of the largest families of any meat-eater on earth: usually five to eight cubs, and in a summer thick with lemmings, more than a dozen.
facts.more: Litter size tracks the food supply. Lemming numbers rise and crash on a cycle of a few years. In a boom summer a mother can raise a dozen or more cubs in one den; in a crash year she may not breed at all.

facts.text: One young female walked from Norway to Canada. Her satellite collar logged 3,506 km (2,179 miles) in 76 days — more than a marathon a day, across drifting sea ice.
facts.more: She left Svalbard in late March, crossed to Greenland in 21 days, and reached Ellesmere Island in Nunavut by June. Her fastest single day covered 155 km (96 miles). Young foxes make journeys like this to find country of their own to live in.

facts.text: Fox dens are handed down. Generation after generation digs the same sandy ridge until it has dozens of entrances — and the plants on top grow greener than anywhere around.
facts.more: Droppings, food scraps and urine build up in the soil over the years and fertilise it, so an old den mound sits on gray tundra like a bright green island. Researchers spot dens from far off just by the color of the grass.

facts.text: In summer it caches. A fox carries goose eggs away one at a time and buries them in cold ground, then digs them up months later when the tundra has nothing left to offer.
facts.more: On Bylot Island in Canada, researchers watched foxes stash hundreds of eggs taken from snow-goose colonies. The frozen soil works like a refrigerator, and the eggs stay edible long enough to feed a fox through the leanest stretch of winter.

facts.text: Follow the biggest hunter and you eat. Arctic foxes shadow polar bears across the sea ice for miles, waiting to clean up the seal the bear leaves behind.
facts.more: A polar bear eats the fat and abandons most of the meat, so a single kill can feed several foxes and a crowd of gulls. Foxes have been tracked far out on floating ice, well beyond sight of land, living entirely on someone else's leftovers.

facts.text: It is smaller than it looks. About house-cat size, roughly 3.5 kg (8 lb) — and a good share of what you see is fur, not fox.

wonder: Fur on the soles of its feet, ears kept small to save heat, a coat that turns white before the snow arrives — every part of this fox is fitted for the cold it was made to live in.

name: Grey wolf
blurb: The largest wild member of the dog family — a long-legged hunter that lives, hunts and raises its young as a family.
size: As tall at the shoulder as a big German shepherd, but longer-legged and heavier-headed

facts.text: A wolf pack is not an army. It is a family — a mother, a father, and their pups from this year and last. The "alpha" fighting his way to the top is a myth.
facts.more: That idea came from watching unrelated wolves crowded into a zoo enclosure, where strangers really do scrap over rank. In the wild the leaders are simply the parents. The biologist whose book spread the alpha story spent years afterwards asking people to stop repeating it.

facts.text: A howl carries about 10 miles (16 km) across open tundra and 6 miles (10 km) through forest. It is how a pack scattered over a hunt finds itself again.
facts.more: Wolves howl to regroup, to rally before a hunt, and to warn neighbouring packs off their ground. Each wolf's voice is distinct enough that packmates can tell who is calling — and a chorus of three or four is very hard to count by ear.

facts.text: Wolves are built for distance, not sprints. A pack may cover 30 miles (50 km) in a day at an easy trot, patrolling a territory bigger than many cities.
facts.more: The trot runs about 5 mph (8 km/h) and they can hold it for hours. Territories range from around 50 square miles to several hundred, and the pack works the boundaries as it goes, leaving scent marks that tell other wolves the ground is taken.

facts.text: Feast or famine. After a kill a wolf can eat 20 lb (9 kg) of meat at one sitting — then go days, sometimes over a week, with nothing at all.
facts.more: Most hunts fail. Wolves test many animals for every one they catch, so when food is finally in front of them they load up completely. That is where the phrase "wolfing it down" comes from, and a wolf leaving a carcass really does look bloated.

facts.text: Behind the long canines sit the carnassials — blade-shaped teeth that pass each other like scissor blades and shear straight through hide, tendon and bone.
facts.more: A wolf has 42 teeth. The canines can top an inch (2.5 cm) and are for gripping; the carnassials do the cutting. Wolves also crack open leg bones to reach the marrow inside, which is why a carcass they have finished with is used up so completely.

facts.text: A wolf hunts with its nose. Researchers following packs have watched them swing off course and head straight for a moose 1.5 miles (2.4 km) away, downwind and out of sight.
Pups are born underground, blind and deaf, weighing about as much as a can of soup. Their eyes open at around two weeks, and the outside world waits a few weeks longer.
Adults eat at the kill, walk miles home, then bring it back up for the pups. The pups start it themselves, nipping and licking at the adult's mouth until it comes.
facts.more: It is the most efficient way to carry 10 lb of meat across rough country — inside you. Any pack member will do it, not just the mother, and the pups mob whichever adult walks into the clearing by the den first.

facts.text: Young wolves strike out alone. One male collared in Oregon walked more than 1,000 miles (1,600 km) across two states, by himself, before he found a mate and settled.
facts.more: He was known only by his collar number, OR-7. Dispersing wolves like him cross highways, rivers and whole mountain ranges searching for empty country and a partner, which is how wolves turn up in places where nobody expected them.

facts.text: A wolf sleeps outdoors in a blizzard, curled nose to tail with that thick brush laid across its face, and simply lets the snow drift over it.
Put your hand inside a wolf track and your palm vanishes. A front paw runs roughly 4 by 5 inches (10 by 13 cm) — far wider than a coyote's, and wider than most dogs of the same height.
facts.more: Broad feet work like snowshoes on soft snow. In deep drifts a pack walks single file, each wolf stepping exactly into the prints of the one ahead, so a line of six can leave a trail that looks like one animal passed through.

wonder: The pack is a family before it is anything else — parents, pups, shared meals, and a voice that carries ten miles to call everyone home.

name: Polar bear
blurb: The largest bear on earth — a white-coated hunter that lives out on Arctic sea ice and hunts seals.
size: Rearing up on its back legs, about as tall as a basketball hoop

facts.text: Stand a big male on his hind legs and he reaches about 10 ft (3 m) — eye to eye with a basketball hoop. He weighs more than eight grown men put together.
facts.more: Males run 350-650 kg (770-1,430 lb); females are roughly half that. For all that bulk, a polar bear walks almost silently, because the soles of its feet are padded and thickly furred between the pads.

facts.text: Polar bear fur is not white. Every guard hair is a clear, hollow tube — and the skin underneath is jet black. You can see the black on its nose and lips.
facts.more: The hollow core scatters sunlight in all directions at once. Because every color scatters equally, your eye adds them back together as white. It is the same reason crushed glass and fresh snow look white while a single piece of either is see-through.

facts.text: A polar bear can smell a seal from more than a kilometer (0.6 miles) away, and through a meter (3 ft) of packed snow — enough to find a seal pup sealed inside a snow lair.
facts.more: Ringed seals hollow out birth lairs under the snow on top of the ice, completely invisible from above. The bear works the wind, walks in carefully, then rears up on its back legs and crashes down through the roof with both front feet.

facts.text: One collared female swam for nine days without stopping — 687 km (426 miles) of open Arctic sea, in water only a few degrees above freezing.
facts.more: A GPS collar and a temperature logger recorded the whole crossing: 232 hours in water of 2-6 C (36-43 F). She lost roughly a fifth of her body weight doing it. Polar bears swim with the front legs only, the back legs trailing behind as rudders.

facts.text: Its front paw is the size of a dinner plate — up to 30 cm (12 in) across. The toes are slightly webbed for paddling, and the soles are covered in papillae, tiny bumps that grip ice.
facts.more: Wide feet spread an enormous weight across thin ice the way snowshoes spread yours across deep snow. Fur fills the gaps between the pads for warmth and extra grip, and the claws are short, thick and curved — ice hooks rather than knives.

facts.text: A polar bear eats the fat first. It can strip 45 kg (100 lb) of blubber off a seal in a single meal, then walk away and leave the red meat for foxes and gulls.
facts.more: Blubber is nearly pure energy, and a bear living on the ice needs energy far more than it needs protein. Arctic foxes trail bears for exactly this reason: one seal kill can feed half a dozen scavengers after the bear has finished with it.

facts.text: A newborn polar bear weighs about 600 g — a grapefruit — blind and thinly furred, born inside a snow cave in the depth of Arctic winter.
facts.more: By the time the family digs its way out in March the cubs weigh around 10 kg, about twenty times their birth weight. Their mother's milk is roughly a third fat, among the richest milk of any bear.

facts.text: The mother digs a den into a snowdrift and shuts herself in for months — no food, no water, no daylight — living off her own fat while the cubs nurse.
facts.more: Inside, the den stays far warmer than the air outside, heated by the bear herself. A pregnant female may go up to eight months without a single meal, from before she dens until she is back out on the ice hunting with cubs at her heels.

facts.text: It can run 25 mph (40 km/h) — but only briefly. That coat is so warm the bear overheats within minutes, so it hunts by waiting rather than chasing.
facts.more: After a short chase, bears have been watched rolling in snow or lying spread out flat on the ice to cool down. Everything that keeps a polar bear alive at -40 works against it the second it starts to run.

facts.text: The still-hunt: find a seal's breathing hole, lie down beside it, and wait — completely motionless, sometimes for hours. Most of the time the seal never comes up.
facts.more: Seals keep several holes open in the ice and surface at whichever one they choose, so the odds are against the bear on any single attempt. Patience is the entire technique. A bear that fidgets goes hungry.

facts.text: It is the only bear counted as a marine mammal. Its scientific name, Ursus maritimus, means "sea bear", and it can spend most of the year out on floating ice, far from any land.

wonder: Hollow hair, black skin, snowshoe feet with the grip built into the soles — a polar bear wears everything the Arctic asks of it.

name: Grizzly bear
blurb: A large brown bear of North America's mountains and salmon rivers, with a hump of muscle on its shoulders and claws built for digging.
size: Standing up, taller than a doorway; a big male outweighs three grown men

facts.text: That hump over its shoulders is solid muscle, and it powers the front legs. A grizzly can dig itself a hole to lie in through ground you would need a pickaxe for.
facts.more: The claws finish the job: 5-10 cm (2-4 in) long and almost straight, shaped for turning over rocks and hauling out roots and ground squirrels. A black bear's claws are shorter and hooked for climbing, which is why black bears go up trees easily and grizzlies mostly do not.

facts.text: By late summer a grizzly goes into hyperphagia — "over-eating". It feeds up to 20 hours a day and can put on 1.5-3 kg (3-6 lb) of fat every single day.
facts.more: The signal that tells the body it is full gets switched off. A bear on a salmon river or a berry slope will eat, doze briefly, and eat again around the clock, because the fat it carries into the den is every calorie it will get until spring.

facts.text: In the den it does not eat, drink, urinate or pass droppings for five to seven months — and walks out in spring with nearly all its muscle still on it.
facts.more: Instead of dumping waste, a denning bear recycles it: urea is broken apart and the nitrogen rebuilt into protein. A human loses serious muscle after only weeks in bed, so doctors study bears closely, hoping to learn how they hold on to theirs.

facts.text: Cubs are born in midwinter, deep in the den, weighing about 450 g (1 lb) — blind, nearly bald, and smaller than their mother's paw.
facts.more: She is in torpor, drowsy rather than fully asleep, and rouses to clean and feed them. Her milk is roughly a third fat, so by the time the family walks out into April light the cubs weigh several kilos and can follow her.

facts.text: A bear's world is smell. The olfactory bulb — the part of the brain that handles scent — is at least five times bigger than yours, and its nose lining has about a hundred times more surface.
facts.more: Inside the muzzle, thin sheets of bone are folded like a honeycomb to pack in all that surface. A grizzly lifts its nose, swings its head slowly, and reads the wind — which is why hikers are told to make noise rather than surprise one at close range.

facts.text: A grizzly runs about 35 mph (56 km/h) — faster than any human ever timed. And no, it does not slow down going downhill.
facts.more: One bear was clocked holding 25-28 mph for two miles. The old advice to run downhill from a bear is simply wrong; they are agile on steep ground. Rangers tell you not to run at all, because running is what turns you into something worth chasing.

facts.text: High in the Rockies, grizzlies climb above the treeline to eat moths. One bear can turn over rock after rock and lick up 40,000 army cutworm moths in a single day.
facts.more: The moths shelter from summer heat in cool piles of broken rock, and their bodies are so fatty that a day of licking them up carries a bear's whole energy needs. Bears walk to the same rock fields year after year and feed close together without much argument.

facts.text: When salmon are thick in the river, a bear stops eating whole fish. It bites out the skin, brain and eggs — the fattiest parts — and drops the rest on the bank.
facts.more: Biologists call it selective feeding, and it only happens when fish are so plentiful the bear can afford the waste. Gulls, eagles and smaller bears finish what is left, and the carcasses dragged into the woods feed the trees along the riverbank.

facts.text: Most years it digs a brand-new den, usually on a steep north-facing slope where snow drifts deep, and the sleeping chamber is often barely bigger than the curled-up bear.
facts.more: A tight den holds body heat. Snow piling over the entrance seals it like a blanket, and the bear may plug the tunnel with branches and grass. Many dens collapse in the spring thaw, which is one reason bears rarely move back into an old one.

facts.text: Inland grizzlies weigh around 200 kg (440 lb). Coastal brown bears with salmon rivers to fish reach twice that. Same animal — different dinner.
facts.more: Kodiak and Alaskan coastal bears can top 450 kg (1,000 lb) because salmon deliver enormous fat in a short season. Inland grizzlies live on roots, grasses, berries, moths and the occasional elk calf: plenty to live on, not enough to grow huge.

facts.text: Bears leave messages on trees. A grizzly backs up to a trunk, rubs hard, and leaves behind hair and scent — and trail cameras show bear after bear visiting the very same tree.

wonder: A whole winter with no food, no water and no waste, and the bear walks out in spring with its strength still on it.

name: Giant panda
blurb: A black-and-white bear from the cold mountain forests of China that eats almost nothing but bamboo.
size: About as heavy as a grown man, on much shorter legs

facts.text: A panda has a spare thumb. It is not a finger at all but an enlarged wrist bone, the radial sesamoid, jutting out under the paw and pressing against the other five.
facts.more: That extra knuckle lets a panda hold a bamboo stem the way you hold a pencil — turning it, stripping leaves, feeding it into the side of its mouth. No other bear has one, and it is why a panda can sit upright and eat with its hands for hours at a time.

facts.text: An adult eats 12-38 kg (26-84 lb) of bamboo a day and spends 12-15 hours doing it. That is more than half of every single day, spent eating.
facts.more: Bamboo is poor fuel: a panda gets only about a sixth of the nutrition out of what it swallows. The only way to make that work is sheer volume, so a panda's life is essentially one long meal broken up by naps.

facts.text: Watch one crunch a stem as thick as your thumb. Broad flat molars and jaw muscles anchored right across a wide skull turn the whole head into a pair of bolt cutters.
facts.more: The panda's famously round face is mostly muscle and heavy bone built for chewing. Its molars are wide and ridged for grinding tough fiber, nothing like the shearing blades of a wolf, and the bite is strong enough to split a bamboo culm lengthways.

facts.text: Bamboo is a grass — but a panda is not built like a grass-eater. It has the canine teeth and the short, simple gut of a meat-eater, and it sits in the order Carnivora alongside wolves.
facts.more: A cow ferments plant food for days in a many-chambered stomach full of microbes. A panda's gut is a plain tube, so bamboo passes through in well under a day, barely broken down. It gets around the problem by eating vast amounts and moving slowly to save energy.

facts.text: Bamboo goes through a panda so fast it comes out still green and shredded. A panda leaves droppings dozens of times a day — and researchers count wild pandas by finding them.
facts.more: Wild panda surveys really are run this way. The chewed bamboo fragments in a dropping come out at different lengths from panda to panda, and DNA carried along with it can identify the individual. A whole national census, built out of droppings.

facts.text: A newborn panda weighs about 100 g — pink, blind, hairless, and roughly one nine-hundredth of its mother. Almost no other mammal is born so tiny beside its own parent.
facts.more: Picture a stick of butter next to a grown man. The mother cradles her cub almost constantly for the first weeks; its eyes do not open for six to eight weeks, and it will not walk properly for months.

facts.text: It bleats. A friendly panda greeting sounds like a goat kid, and pandas also honk, chirp, huff and bark. What no panda ever does is roar.
facts.more: Researchers have sorted panda calls into about a dozen types. A bleat is friendly, a honk means mild annoyance, and chirping between adults in spring is a male and female trying to locate each other in bamboo so dense neither can see more than a few meters.

facts.text: A male marks trees by doing a handstand — walking his back feet up the trunk so he can spray urine as high as he can possibly reach.
facts.more: A higher mark carries further on the breeze and lasts longer before rain washes it off, and it tells any panda passing roughly how big the animal that left it was. Pandas pick big trees with rough bark for the job, because rough bark holds the scent.

facts.text: Pandas do not hibernate. When mountain winter closes in, a panda simply walks downhill to where the bamboo is still standing green, and carries on eating.
facts.more: Bamboo does not die back the way most plants do, so there is food all year. A panda could not store enough fat to sleep through winter anyway — its diet never leaves a surplus. Instead it has the coat for it: coarse, oily fur that sheds rain and snow.

facts.text: Between meals it sleeps two to four hours wherever it happens to be — flat on its back, draped over a fallen log, or wedged into the fork of a tree.
A panda cub climbs before it can fight. Cubs go straight up a trunk to escape trouble, and even adults, heavy as they are, can haul themselves into the branches.

wonder: A bear that lives on grass, given the one extra thumb it needs to hold it.
